title: Discrete hedging
text:
An option carries a probability density. A portfolio of stock and cash carries another. Hedging asks how closely the second can reproduce the first. Exact agreement means replication; a remaining difference records the exposures the available portfolio cannot match.
The options page plots distributions over observations at expiry. Here the question is local: what can a portfolio reproduce between now and the next trading date? All prices are in units of \(Y\), so the reference asset has value one.

title: Discrete hedging
text:
One trading interval
Suppose the stock is worth \(x=X(t)\) today, the call expires in \(\tau=T-t\) years, and the next rebalance is in \(h\) years, with \(0<h\leq\tau\). In the normal model, a standard normal shock \(z\) produces the stock multiplier
\[
R(h,z)=\exp\!\left\{\sigma\sqrt h\,z-\tfrac12\sigma^2h\right\}.
\]
Under the pricing measure, the shock has density \(q(z)=\varphi(z)\). The stock’s conditional density is therefore
\[
p(z)=R(h,z)\varphi(z).
\]
Both integrate to one: \(\mathbb E^Y[R(h,Z)]=1\). The plotted horizontal axis is the same standardized shock for every density. These are distributions over the next interval’s information, not histograms of hedging errors.
Write \(C(x,\tau)\) for the Black–Scholes call value at current stock price \(x\) and remaining maturity \(\tau\). At the next trading date, its value is \(C(xR(h,z),\tau-h)\). Consequently the call’s conditional density is
\[
c(z)=
\frac{C(xR(h,z),\tau-h)}{C(x,\tau)}
\varphi(z).
\]
Before expiry, the numerator is the remaining option value, rather than its terminal payoff. At \(h=\tau\), it becomes \((xR(h,z)-K)^+\). Conditional pricing ensures that this density also integrates to one.

title: Discrete hedging
section: A target that includes a reserve
text:
A target that includes a reserve
The explorer can hedge a call together with a fixed reserve \(B\geq0\) in \(Y\). Its current value is
\[
H=C(x,\tau)+B.
\]
Its density over the next interval becomes
\[
c_B(z)=
\frac{C(xR(h,z),\tau-h)+B}{H}
\varphi(z).
\]
The default uses \(B=K\): the terminal target is \((X(T)-K)^++K=\max(X(T),K)\), a stock position with a protected floor. This is also a put plus the stock by put–call parity.
Adding the reserve changes the target payoff as well as its price. It makes the target less concentrated in upside states; it does not supply a cost-free improvement to the original call hedge.
Spend a fraction \(w\) of the same budget \(H\) on stock and keep the rest in \(Y\). Hold that position until the next trading date. Its value and density are
\[
V(t+h,z)=H\{1-w+wR(h,z)\},
\]
\[
v(w,z)=\{1-w+wR(h,z)\}\varphi(z).
\]
This is a cost-weighted mixture of the stock and reference densities. The share holding is \(\Delta(t)=Hw/x\); the cost fraction \(w\) and the number of shares \(\Delta(t)\) are different quantities.

title: Discrete hedging
section: Move the hedge toward the target
text:
Move the hedge toward the target
Start with the call plus a reserve equal to the strike, then press Fit the density. Change the time to the next rebalance and compare the two curves. Finally select Call only to see why the positivity constraint matters.

The interactive density comparison requires JavaScript. For a stock price of 100, strike of 110, annual volatility 30%, and one year remaining, the call costs about 8.14 and its Black–Scholes delta is about 0.433 shares. With a 110-unit reserve the target costs 118.14; the corresponding delta cost fraction is about 0.367.

The fitted position minimizes the forward relative entropy
\[
w^\star=\underset{0\leq w\leq1}{\arg\min}\;
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(c_B\Vert v(w)),
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
&D_{\mathrm{KL}}(c_B\Vert v(w))\\
&\quad=\int c_B(z)\log\frac{c_B(z)}{v(w,z)}\,dz.
\end{aligned}
\]
Zero divergence means identical densities, hence identical next-date values for the same initial cost. Positive divergence measures the remaining mismatch in nats. It is also the loss of expected log performance, evaluated under the target measure, relative to holding the target itself.
The optimization is convex in \(w\). The figure compares its best value with the chosen position over several interval lengths. Shorter intervals change the local problem: they do not simply add more points to the same terminal distribution.

title: Discrete hedging
section: Why the call-only fit reaches a boundary
text:
Why the call-only fit reaches a boundary
In the normal model, the next stock multiplier can be arbitrarily close to zero or arbitrarily large. A position held unchanged over a finite interval must satisfy
\[
1-w+wR\geq0
\qquad\text{for every }R>0.
\]
With only stock and cash, that condition is exactly \(0\leq w\leq1\). Borrowing cash would give \(w>1\), and sufficiently large downward moves would then make the portfolio negative. Shorting the stock would fail in the other tail. A negative function cannot be used as a probability density.
For the default call without a reserve, Black–Scholes delta requires about 0.433 shares, costing about 43.34, while the call itself costs only 8.14. Its stock cost fraction is about 5.32: the rest is financed by borrowing. The finite-step positive-density fit cannot take that position. The Call only preset makes the restriction visible by putting the best admissible fit at the all-stock boundary.
This does not contradict continuous-time replication. A continuously rebalanced strategy changes its position as the stock moves. It is a different admissibility problem from a leveraged position left unchanged across a finite interval.

title: Discrete hedging
text:
Where Black–Scholes delta reappears
For the call plus a fixed reserve, the derivative with respect to stock price is still the call delta:
\[
\Delta^{\mathrm{BS}}(t)=\Phi(d(1)).
\]
\[
w^{\mathrm{BS}}=\frac{x\Phi(d(1))}{H}.
\]
The options page defines \(d(1)\) and derives the Black–Scholes formula from two normal tail probabilities. When this cost fraction is strictly inside the admissible interval, the short-interval KL fit approaches the same delta. The default reserve is large enough for this condition to hold. Press Fit the density, then reduce \(h\) to see the fitted share holding approach the delta benchmark.
The book also develops two quadratic hedges: a target-relative weighted error criterion, and the classical minimum-variance criterion. Their finite-step positions need not agree. In the normal model, both approach delta as the interval shrinks. The direct KL fit shown here retains the full logarithmic objective and its positivity restriction.






NoteWhat is being calculated





The lab solves one conditional trading interval at the current stock price. A strategy on a trading grid repeats that calculation after each observed move, using the new stock price and remaining maturity. The graphs do not claim to show a complete multistep replication or a realized hedge profit.
The integrals use deterministic numerical quadrature over standard normal shocks, with a separate breakpoint at the strike when the interval reaches expiry. The plotted range contains nearly all the probability mass for these controls; numerical integration uses a wider range. Zero target density contributes zero to forward KL. The normal family and volatility range keep the integration well behaved.









NoteBook connection





Based on Chapter 6 of Jan Vecer’s Principles of Portfolio Choice: An Information-Theoretic, Likelihood-Based Perspective: local Kullback–Leibler projection, cost weights versus hedge shares, the normal model’s discrete call hedges, and the full-support positivity restriction. The reserve is an explicit target modification that makes an interior stock-and-cash comparison possible.

title: Portfolio laboratory
text:
A desired probability distribution need not be attainable with the assets a market offers. The trinomial model makes that restriction visible. This laboratory turns it into a portfolio problem: enter the distributions carried by the available assets, then find their best mixture for your belief.
This is a finite-state, one-period model. Every number describes the same scenario and horizon, and all prices and payoffs use the same reference asset \(Y\).

title: Portfolio laboratory
section: A portfolio is a mixture of measures
text:
A portfolio is a mixture of measures
Write \(q_i=\mathbb P^Y(i)>0\) for market pricing probabilities, \(p_i=\mathbb P^M(i)\) for beliefs, and \(a_{ji}=\mathbb P^{A_j}(i)\) for the distribution carried by asset \(j\). A unit of initial wealth invested in that asset pays
\[
G^j(i)=\frac{a_{ji}}{q_i}.
\]
Allocate cost weights \(w_j\geq0\) with \(\sum_jw_j=1\). The portfolio’s distribution is
\[
v_i=\sum_jw_ja_{ji},
\]
and its gross payoff is
\[
G(i)=\frac{v_i}{q_i}.
\]
The weights are fractions of the initial budget, not numbers of shares. If the initial asset price is \(A_j(0)\) and total wealth is \(W\), the holding is \(w_jW/A_j(0)\) units. A reference-asset holding has density \(a_{0i}=q_i\) and gross payoff one.

title: Portfolio laboratory
section: Enter a market and a belief
text:
Enter a market and a belief
Each row is a distribution across the same states. For example, “state 1” must mean the same outcome in the market row, belief row and every asset row. The table accepts 2–12 states and up to eight risky asset distributions; the reference asset is always available. Apply the inputs to normalize proportional weights explicitly. The market row must remain strictly positive; beliefs and asset rows may contain zeros.
Start with the book’s incomplete three-state example, solve for log growth, and inspect the residual mismatch. Then try the four-state menu or the fully spanned state-claim preset. You can also change an asset density or add another asset. A larger menu can improve the best attainable growth, but it need not change the optimum if the added asset provides no useful new exposure.




Interactive portfolio laboratory. It needs JavaScript.



Figure 1: Editable pricing, belief and asset distributions. The solver chooses long-only cost weights. The displayed density and payoff describe the same portfolio; its expected log growth is always evaluated under the belief row, whichever optimization criterion is selected.









TipA useful three-step experiment




Solve with the default asset menu. Inspect where the implemented distribution misses the belief.
Add an asset whose distribution equals your belief. Under exact log optimization, the mismatch can now reach zero.
Change that asset so it no longer matches. Compare the exact log and quadratic solutions, then inspect their statewise payoffs.

title: Portfolio laboratory
text:
What the exact solver minimizes
Use \(D(P\Vert Q)\) for KL divergence. Expected log growth satisfies
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E^M[\log G]&=D(p\Vert q)\\
&\quad-D(p\Vert v).
\end{aligned}
\]
For fixed prices and beliefs, the first term is constant. The exact problem is therefore
\[
\min_{w\in\Delta}\;D\bigl(p\Vert v(w)\bigr),
\]
where \(\Delta\) is the simplex of nonnegative weights summing to one.
The feasible distributions form the convex hull of the asset rows. The optimizer finds the closest point in that set in the stated direction of KL divergence. Reversing the arguments would solve a different problem.
If \(p\) lies in the hull, the full likelihood-ratio payoff is attainable. If it lies outside, the minimum divergence is the exact amount of expected log growth lost because of the restricted menu. The portfolio measure may be unique even when several weight vectors implement it.






NoteWhy this optimization is convex





Ignoring a constant independent of \(w\), the objective is
\[
-\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\log v_i.
\]
Each \(v_i\) is linear in \(w\), and \(-\log\) is convex. The simplex of nonnegative weights summing to one is a convex feasible set. A valid first-order optimum is therefore globally optimal within this menu and these constraints.
For finite growth, every state with \(p_i>0\) needs \(v_i>0\). If all available assets assign zero mass to such a state, every allocation has expected log growth \(-\infty\). Including the reference asset guarantees a feasible portfolio with finite growth.

title: Portfolio laboratory
text:
Read the numerical result
The reported expected growth uses natural logarithms, so it is measured in nats over the chosen horizon. It is model-implied expected log return, not a promised return and not automatically an annual rate. The payoff table provides the statewise outcomes that produce it.
A numerical optimum is assessed by its first-order gap. For exact log growth, define the marginal improvement of asset \(j\) by
\[
b_j=\sum_{i:p_i>0}\frac{p_ia_{ji}}{v_i}.
\]
At a finite feasible portfolio, \(\sum_jw_jb_j=1\). The gap
\[
\delta=\max_jb_j-1
\]
bounds the remaining possible improvement in expected log growth. A small gap certifies that the current allocation is close to the global optimum in objective value. It does not guarantee that every individual weight is close to a unique target; redundant assets can give many equivalent portfolios.

title: Portfolio laboratory
section: Why the quadratic solution can differ
text:
Why the quadratic solution can differ
The laboratory offers exact log growth, the book’s mixed quadratic and classical mean–variance. The mean–variance page also explains their relation to the ordinary Taylor approximation. Exact log growth minimizes \(D(p\Vert v)\). The mixed quadratic minimizes
\[
\frac12\sum_i\frac{(v_i-p_i)^2}{q_i}.
\]
Classical mean–variance instead uses the portfolio mean and covariance under the subjective measure. It has a separate risk-penalty parameter. These are different objectives on the same feasible set; comparing their exact log growth afterward makes the consequences visible.
Long-only mixtures guarantee a nonnegative payoff and make the feasible set easy to interpret. Short selling would enlarge the set to affine combinations, with an additional statewise constraint to keep the payoff nonnegative. That extension changes the feasible geometry and is outside this laboratory.
Continue: options provide concrete asset-density shapes that can serve as portfolio ingredients. Utility and fractional Kelly explain how a preference or reserve rule changes the target portfolio.






NoteBook connection





Based on Chapter 1 of Jan Vecer’s Principles of Portfolio Choice: An Information-Theoretic, Likelihood-Based Perspective, especially the theorem “State price density of a general static portfolio,” together with the constrained portfolio problems and information projections in Chapter 3. The finite-state laboratory illustrates these constructions without introducing a dynamic trading rule.

title: Utility & fractional Kelly
text:
The framework gives a direct payoff for a belief: invest in the likelihood ratio \(R=\mathbb P^M/\mathbb P^Y\). That position maximizes expected log growth under the stated belief. It does not answer how much wealth an investor wants to expose to that belief, or which other preferences she might have.
Two familiar responses fit into the same language. Expected utility chooses a transformed payoff. Fractional Kelly allocates part of the budget to the original likelihood-ratio payoff and keeps the rest in the reference asset.
All wealth on this page is measured in units of the reference asset \(Y\). The formulas first describe a complete, finite-state market with positive pricing probabilities. Restricted asset menus require a further optimization over attainable portfolios.

title: Utility & fractional Kelly
text:
What utility maximization does
Let \(W\) be initial wealth and \(V(T)\) the terminal payoff. An investor with increasing, strictly concave utility \(U\) solves
\[
\max_{V(T)\geq0}\;\mathbb E^M[U(V(T))]
\]
subject to the pricing constraint
\[
\mathbb E^Y[V(T)]=W.
\]
Write \(p_i=\mathbb P^M(i)\) and \(q_i=\mathbb P^Y(i)\). An extra unit paid in state \(i\) contributes \(p_iU'(V(T,i))\) to expected utility and costs \(q_i\). At an interior optimum, the marginal utility per unit of cost is the same in every state with \(p_i>0\):
\[
U'(V^*(T,i))=\lambda\frac{q_i}{p_i}.
\]
If \(I=(U')^{-1}\) is inverse marginal utility, then
\[
V^*(T,i)=I\!\left(\lambda\frac{q_i}{p_i}\right).
\]
The budget fixes \(\lambda\). The resulting portfolio still induces a probability distribution,
\[
v_i^*=q_i\frac{V^*(T,i)}{W}.
\]
Utility therefore supplies a rule for turning the investor’s belief \(p\) and the market’s prices \(q\) into the implemented measure \(v^*\).






NoteConditions behind the formula





The inverse-marginal-utility formula applies when \(U\) is continuously differentiable and strictly concave, with \(U'(0+)=\infty\) and \(U'(\infty)=0\). In the finite-state setting, a positive budget determines the multiplier uniquely. A state with \(p_i=0\) contributes nothing to the objective; paying it a positive amount would consume budget, so the optimizer assigns it zero. Utility at zero is interpreted through the boundary limit, and states of zero subjective probability do not enter the expectation.

title: Utility & fractional Kelly
section: CRRA: a power of the likelihood ratio
text:
CRRA: a power of the likelihood ratio
Constant relative risk aversion uses
\[
U_\gamma(x)=\frac{x^{1-\gamma}-1}{1-\gamma},
\]
with \(U_1(x)=\log x\). Set \(\alpha=1/\gamma\) and \(R(i)=p_i/q_i\). The optimal gross payoff is
\[
G^U(i)=\frac{R(i)^\alpha}{\sum_jq_jR(j)^\alpha}.
\]
Its implied probabilities are
\[
v^U(i)=q_iG^U(i).
\]
At \(\gamma=1\), \(G^U=R\) and \(v^U=p\): utility reproduces the full Kelly position. For \(\gamma>1\), the power moderates the likelihood ratios. The denominator is essential: it makes the payoff cost exactly one unit of initial wealth.
For positive \(p_i\) in every state, increasing \(\gamma\) eventually brings the implemented measure back to \(q\). This is normalized geometric interpolation between the two distributions.

title: Utility & fractional Kelly
text:
Fractional Kelly: keep a reserve
Invest a fraction \(f\in[0,1]\) of wealth in the full Kelly payoff and leave \(1-f\) in \(Y\). The gross terminal payoff is
\[
G^F(i)=(1-f)+fR(i).
\]
Multiplication by \(q_i\) gives
\[
v^F(i)=(1-f)q_i+fp_i.
\]
The original belief still determines the active position. The total portfolio’s measure is an arithmetic mixture because part of the budget stays in reserve. In particular,
\[
G^F(i)\geq1-f.
\]
This is a terminal wealth floor in units of \(Y\). With \(f=0.25\), at least three quarters of initial wealth remains even if the active position pays zero. It is not a claim about purchasing power in another unit, or about every strategy called “fractional Kelly.” Here the definition is a static holding of the reference asset and the full Kelly claim, without repeated rebalancing to a fixed risky weight.

title: Utility & fractional Kelly
text:
Compare the two portfolios
Start with \(\gamma=2\) and \(f=1/2\). Compare the state probabilities and the payoff floor. Keep the fraction linked to \(1/\gamma\) for a matched-parameter comparison, or unlink it to choose the reserve independently. Then increase risk aversion and try a belief that assigns zero probability to one state. The three-state view makes the difference between arithmetic and geometric interpolation visible.




Interactive comparison. It needs JavaScript.



Figure 1: The same market prices and subjective belief generate two moderated portfolios. Their expected log growth is evaluated under the original belief \(\mathbb P^M\); it is not the CRRA objective. The simplex shows the three probabilities as a single point.



The choice \(f=1/\gamma\) is a useful comparison, not a general equivalence. For beliefs close to prices, both gross payoffs have the same first-order expansion:
\[
G\approx1+\frac{R-1}{\gamma}.
\]
Further from the market distribution, their shapes and downside protection can differ substantially.






NoteWhy two states can conceal the difference



With two states and strictly positive beliefs, both families cover the segment from \(q\) to \(p\) for \(\gamma\geq1\), including cash as a limit. One allocation can be matched by a different parameter in the other family. They generally disagree at the same numerical \(\gamma\). With three or more states, they generally follow different curves, so changing one scalar parameter need not match the portfolios.








NoteWhat happens when a belief is zero?





For every finite \(\gamma\), CRRA retains the zero wherever \(p_i=0\). Fractional Kelly with \(f<1\) assigns that state positive mass through the reserve.
Let \(B=\{i:p_i>0\}\). As \(\gamma\to\infty\), the CRRA probabilities converge to
\[
v^U(i)\longrightarrow
\frac{q_i\mathbf1_B(i)}{\sum_{j\in B}q_j}.
\]
Thus the cash limit requires full subjective support. Otherwise the limit is the pricing distribution conditioned on the states the investor considers possible.

title: Utility & fractional Kelly
text:
The information cost of moderation
Write \(D(P\Vert Q)\) for relative entropy and let \(v\) be either implemented distribution. The growth decomposition gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E^M[\log G]&=D(p\Vert q)\\
&\quad-D(p\Vert v).
\end{aligned}
\]
The difference from full Kelly is exactly the mismatch \(D(p\Vert v)\). That loss of expected log growth can be an intentional choice made for another objective or a wealth floor. It is measured under the stated belief; changing the belief can change the ranking.
Continue: explore mean–variance approximations, or choose among available assets in the portfolio laboratory.






NoteBook connection





Based on Chapter 3 of Jan Vecer’s Principles of Portfolio Choice: An Information-Theoretic, Likelihood-Based Perspective: “Utility Maximization” and “Risk aversion: utility-based density tempering versus fractional Kelly sizing.” The normal model shows how these constructions behave for Gaussian likelihoods.

title: Gamma: accumulated activity
text:
The Poisson model counts isolated events. A gamma driver records a nonnegative amount of accumulated activity. It could represent an abstract operational clock or accumulated volume; the financial interpretation requires a model linking that quantity to the application.
The driver increases by jumps. Although its value at any fixed positive time has a continuous density, its paths are not continuous: a gamma process has infinitely many small jumps on every positive time interval.

title: Gamma: accumulated activity
text:
Common shape, different rates
Specify one additive driver \(G(t)\) under two measures:
\[
\begin{aligned}
G(t)&\sim\Gamma(\alpha t,\beta_X)
&&\text{under }\mathbb P^X,\\
G(t)&\sim\Gamma(\alpha t,\beta_Y)
&&\text{under }\mathbb P^Y.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(\alpha>0\) is the common shape rate. The parameters \(\beta_X,\beta_Y>0\) are rates, so the means and variances are
\[
E^j[G(t)]=\frac{\alpha t}{\beta_j},
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}^j[G(t)]=\frac{\alpha t}{\beta_j^2}.
\]
For \(z>0\) and \(j\in\{X,Y\}\), the density is
\[
f_j(z,t)=\frac{\beta_j^{\alpha t}}{\Gamma(\alpha t)}
z^{\alpha t-1}e^{-\beta_jz}.
\]
The common power of \(z\) and the gamma-function factor cancel. The resulting price is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}
&=\left(\frac{\beta_X}{\beta_Y}\right)^{\alpha t}
e^{(\beta_Y-\beta_X)G(t)},\\
\log\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}&=aG(t)+bt,
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
a=\beta_Y-\beta_X,
\qquad b=\alpha\log\frac{\beta_X}{\beta_Y}.
\]
The common shape is essential for this affine expression. Different shape rates would leave an additional \(\log G(t)\) term.

title: Gamma: accumulated activity
text:
Explore the model
The figure fixes \(\beta_Y=2\). Choose the common shape rate, forward information rate and jump direction; the corresponding \(\beta_X\) is then determined. The displayed horizon is at least \(0.5\) and \(\alpha\ge2\), keeping the horizon density finite at zero. This is an exploration range, not a restriction on the mathematical gamma family.

The interactive model requires JavaScript. The default common shape rate is \(\alpha=3\), the pricing rate is \(\beta_Y=2\) and the forward information rate is \(k=0.05\) nats per time unit.

title: Gamma: accumulated activity
text:
Driver jumps become price jumps
For a driver jump of size \(\Delta G(t)>0\),
\[
\frac{X(t)}{X(t-)}=e^{a\Delta G(t)}.
\]
If \(\beta_X>\beta_Y\), the asset measure favors smaller amounts of activity. An upward jump in observed activity then produces a downward price jump, while \(b>0\) supplies the compensating deterministic component. If \(\beta_X<\beta_Y\), the price jumps upward and \(b<0\).
There is no positive interval free of all gamma jumps. The decomposition \(aG(t)+bt\) still separates the jump contribution from the deterministic contribution, but it should not be described as a succession of isolated jumps with empty waiting periods.
The jump intensity density under measure \(\mathbb P^j\) is
\[
\nu_j(dz)=\alpha z^{-1}e^{-\beta_jz}\,dz,
\qquad z>0.
\]
Its integral diverges near zero, giving infinite activity. The integral of jump size against this density is finite, so total accumulated jump size is finite over bounded intervals.

title: Gamma: accumulated activity
text:
Information accumulated per unit time
Taking the mean of the affine log likelihood gives the divergence between the two observation laws at horizon \(t\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
D(\mathbb P^X\Vert\mathbb P^Y)&=k_Xt,\\
k_X&=\alpha\left[
\log\frac{\beta_X}{\beta_Y}
-1+\frac{\beta_Y}{\beta_X}\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
Reversing the two measures gives
\[
k_Y=\alpha\left[
\log\frac{\beta_Y}{\beta_X}
-1+\frac{\beta_X}{\beta_Y}\right].
\]
The expected log-price slopes are \(+k_X\) under \(\mathbb P^X\) and \(-k_Y\) under \(\mathbb P^Y\). The price ratio itself remains a mean-one martingale under \(\mathbb P^Y\).

title: Gamma: accumulated activity
section: From discrete blocks to an additive clock
text:
From discrete blocks to an additive clock
The negative-binomial model sums independent geometric blocks. Gamma laws supply a continuous-valued analogue: independent gamma variables with the same rate add their shape parameters,
\[
\begin{gathered}
\Gamma(\alpha s,\beta)+\Gamma(\alpha t,\beta)\\
\overset{d}{=}\ \Gamma(\alpha(s+t),\beta).
\end{gathered}
\]
For integer shape, a gamma variable is a sum of exponential waiting times. Positive noninteger shapes extend that family consistently to every time increment. The simulation uses these exact increment distributions; the connecting segments do not reproduce the infinitely many individual jumps.
Continue: the inverse Gaussian model gives another additive positive clock, with a different density and a stronger small-jump singularity.






NoteSource and conventions





Jan Vecer, Principles of Portfolio Choice: An Information-Theoretic, Likelihood-Based Perspective, Chapter 5, “Gamma family.” Shape–rate convention: \(\Gamma(s,\beta)\) has mean \(s/\beta\). All prices are in units of \(Y\); \(\mathbb P^X\) and an investor’s \(\mathbb P^M\) are distinct unless explicitly identified.

title: Normal → geometric Brownian motion
text:
The binomial model turns two probabilities into two price multipliers. The normal model does the same with two densities. Start with two normal laws for one observation; their ratio produces geometric Brownian motion exactly.
Throughout, \(X(t)\) is measured in units of the reference asset \(Y\). The pricing measure is \(\mathbb P^Y\); the asset-induced measure is \(\mathbb P^X\). An investor’s belief \(\mathbb P^M\) remains a separate choice.

title: Normal → geometric Brownian motion
text:
One driver, two normal laws
Let \(R(t)\) have independent increments and a common variance rate \(s^2>0\), but different mean rates:
\[
\begin{aligned}
R(t)&\sim N(\mu_Yt,s^2t)
&&\text{under }\mathbb P^Y,\\
R(t)&\sim N(\mu_Xt,s^2t)
&&\text{under }\mathbb P^X.
\end{aligned}
\]
At each horizon \(t>0\), write the two densities with the same formula, for \(j\in\{X,Y\}\):
\[
f_j(z,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi s^2t}}
\exp\!\left[-\frac{(z-\mu_jt)^2}{2s^2t}\right].
\]
The normalizing constants cancel in their ratio. Expanding the two squares leaves a straight line in \(z\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log\frac{f_X(z,t)}{f_Y(z,t)}
&=-\frac{(z-\mu_Xt)^2}{2s^2t}\\
&\quad+\frac{(z-\mu_Yt)^2}{2s^2t}\\
&=az+bt,
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
a=\frac{\mu_X-\mu_Y}{s^2},
\qquad
b=-\frac{\mu_X^2-\mu_Y^2}{2s^2}.
\]
Consequently, the price is already determined:
\[
\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}=\exp\{aR(t)+bt\}.
\]
This is linear information flow: log price is affine in the observed statistic and time. Linear information flow does not mean that price or the driver follows a straight path.

title: Normal → geometric Brownian motion
text:
Explore the model
The figure fixes \(s=1\) and \(\mu_Y=0\). Choose the information rate \(k\); the other mean follows as \(\mu_X=\sqrt{2k}\). The densities, price response and paths all use the same parameters.

The interactive model requires JavaScript. With \(k=0.05\), the driver mean rates are \(0\) and \(\sqrt{0.1}\), the price volatility is \(\sqrt{0.1}\), and the expected log-price rates are \(+0.05\) under \(\mathbb P^X\) and \(-0.05\) under \(\mathbb P^Y\).

title: Normal → geometric Brownian motion
text:
Recover the classical GBM solution
Under the pricing measure, write \(R(t)=\mu_Yt+sW^Y(t)\) and define the signed price loading
\[
\eta=\frac{\mu_X-\mu_Y}{s}.
\]
Substitution into the likelihood ratio gives
\[
\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}
=\exp\!\left\{\eta W^Y(t)-\frac12\eta^2t\right\}.
\]
This is exactly the solution of the discounted geometric Brownian motion equation
\[
\frac{dX(t)}{X(t)}=\eta\,dW^Y(t).
\]
Under the asset measure, \(R(t)=\mu_Xt+sW^X(t)\) instead, so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}
&=\exp\!\left\{\eta W^X(t)+\frac12\eta^2t\right\},\\
\frac{dX(t)}{X(t)}
&=\eta^2dt+\eta\,dW^X(t).
\end{aligned}
\]
The price volatility is \(|\eta|\), not generally the driver scale \(s\). The information rate is \(k=\eta^2/2\), with units of nats per time unit. Volatility and information rate therefore have different units. The book’s convenient normalization \(\mu_Y=0\), \(\mu_X=s^2\) makes \(a=1\) and \(|\eta|=s\); that equality follows from the normalization.

title: Normal → geometric Brownian motion
section: The same model, read in the other direction
text:
The same model, read in the other direction







Dynamics first
Likelihood first




Specify the pricing-measure GBM equation.
Specify two normal laws with a common variance.


Solve for the exponential price.
Divide the two densities.


Recover the asset measure by the price tilt.
Read off the GBM equation if desired.



The two routes give the same process. A differential equation makes local evolution explicit. The likelihood formulation makes the pair of measures and the finite-horizon price formula explicit.

title: Normal → geometric Brownian motion
section: Information is the drift of log price
text:
Information is the drift of log price
The two divergences are equal in this same-variance normal family. In the formulas below, the measures describe observations through the chosen horizon \(t\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
D(\mathbb P^X\Vert\mathbb P^Y)&=kt,\\
D(\mathbb P^Y\Vert\mathbb P^X)&=kt,\\
k&=\frac{(\mu_X-\mu_Y)^2}{2s^2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Accordingly, expected log price is \(+kt\) under \(\mathbb P^X\) and \(-kt\) under \(\mathbb P^Y\). Meanwhile the expected price under \(\mathbb P^Y\) remains \(X(0)\). A mean-zero price return and a negative expected log return are compatible.
The model is consistent at every time scale: increments over a period \(\Delta t\) are normal with mean \(\mu_j\Delta t\) and variance \(s^2\Delta t\). Refining the observation grid changes the view of a path, not the model’s horizon law.
The same two normal laws also give Black–Scholes prices and option densities. For a portfolio held between trading dates, discrete hedging compares its density with the target claim’s density.
Continue: replace continuous fluctuations with counted events in the Poisson model, or return to the shared construction in linear information flow.






NoteSource and conventions





Jan Vecer, Principles of Portfolio Choice: An Information-Theoretic, Likelihood-Based Perspective, Chapter 5, “Normal family (Brownian driver).” This page uses \(s\) for driver scale and \(\eta\) for price loading to keep their roles distinct. All prices are denominated in \(Y\).

title: The trinomial model
text:
The binomial model has just enough traded payoffs to distinguish its two states. A third state exposes two separate issues: which pricing measure fits the traded returns, and which investor beliefs can be implemented by trading?
Work in units of \(Y\) and take the book’s three-state stock return:
\[
R^X=\left(\frac32,1,\frac12\right).
\]
Only \(X\) and \(Y\) are traded. Every state is possible; borrowing and short selling are available unless a portfolio constraint is explicitly imposed.

title: The trinomial model
section: First, find all consistent pricing measures
text:
First, find all consistent pricing measures
The pricing weights must satisfy
\[
q_1+q_2+q_3=1,
\]
\[
\frac32q_1+q_2+\frac12q_3=1.
\]
Subtracting these equations gives \(q_1=q_3\). Thus the positive pricing measures form a line:
\[
\mathbb P^Y(t)=(t,1-2t,t),
\qquad 0<t<\frac12.
\]
Each choice gives an asset measure by multiplying the pricing weights by the stock return:
\[
\mathbb P^X(t)
=\left(\frac{3t}{2},1-2t,\frac t2\right).
\]
Both martingale checks now hold:
\[
\mathbb E^Y[R^X]=1,
\qquad
\mathbb E^X[1/R^X]=1.
\]
The first prices \(X\) in units of \(Y\). The second prices \(Y\) in units of \(X\). Choosing another \(t\) changes both measures while preserving the same stock returns.

title: The trinomial model
text:
Then choose an attainable portfolio
Put a fraction \(w\) of initial wealth in \(X\), and \(1-w\) in \(Y\). Its return is
\[
R^{V,w}
=\left(1+\frac w2,1,1-\frac w2\right).
\]
For a fixed pricing measure, its implied density is
\[
\mathbb P^{V,w}
=(1-w)\mathbb P^Y+w\mathbb P^X.
\]
With no short sales, \(0\le w\le1\): the investor can move along a line segment in the probability triangle. Allowing borrowing and short selling extends the line; nonnegative terminal wealth imposes \(-2\le w\le2\). Neither case fills the triangle.

The interactive figure requires JavaScript. At the book’s default \(t=1/3\), the pricing measure is \((1/3,1/3,1/3)\) and the stock measure is \((1/2,1/3,1/6)\). Every stock-and-cash portfolio retains middle-state probability \(1/3\).

The left triangle varies the pricing rule, holding the stock’s returns fixed. The right triangle varies the portfolio, holding the selected pricing rule fixed. Each corner represents all probability concentrated on one state; interior points assign weight to all three.

title: The trinomial model
section: Why a belief can be unattainable
text:
Why a belief can be unattainable
At the book’s choice \(t=1/3\),
\[
\mathbb P^{V,w}
=\left(\frac{2+w}{6},\frac13,\frac{2-w}{6}\right).
\]
Now consider the investor’s beliefs
\[
\mathbb P^M=\left(\frac12,\frac16,\frac13\right).
\]
Every attainable portfolio has middle-state weight \(1/3\), while the investor assigns \(1/6\). No choice of \(w\) can make the two distributions equal. The unrestricted likelihood payoff \(\mathbb P^M/\mathbb P^Y\) exists as a mathematical claim, but it cannot be replicated using only this stock and cash.
The best attainable portfolio instead minimizes
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb P^M\Vert\mathbb P^{V,w}).
\]
Equivalently, it maximizes
\[
\begin{aligned}
g(w)&=\frac12\log\left(1+\frac w2\right)\\
&\quad+\frac13\log\left(1-\frac w2\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
Here the maximizing weight is \(w=2/5\), under either of the displayed constraints. The figure shows its remaining information mismatch. This weight depends on the beliefs and the traded returns, so it stays the same as \(t\) changes. The two divergences in the growth decomposition change together.






NoteA useful special case



At \(t=5/12\), this particular belief lies on the attainable line and the mismatch vanishes at \(w=2/5\). The market remains incomplete: implementing one selected belief does not mean that every payoff is spanned.

title: The trinomial model
section: Incompleteness also leaves a price range
text:
Incompleteness also leaves a price range
A claim paying one in the middle state and zero otherwise would have price
\[
C(0)=\mathbb P^Y(\omega_2)=1-2t.
\]
The original stock and cash prices permit every value in \((0,1)\). This is an open no-arbitrage interval; its endpoints are limiting bounds, not admissible prices when all three states remain possible. Trading that additional claim at a price inside the interval would identify \(t\) and complete this one-period market.
This is the distinction behind the fundamental theorem of asset pricing: no arbitrage gives existence of a pricing measure; completeness gives uniqueness. A likelihood description respects the same distinction.






TipRead alongside the book



Jan Vecer, Principles of Portfolio Choice: An Information-Theoretic, Likelihood-Based Perspective, Chapter 1, “Trinomial model” and “Numerical trinomial mixture: rigid asset densities”; Chapter 3, incomplete markets and relative-entropy projection.

title: Linear information flow
text:
The binomial, negative binomial, normal, Poisson, gamma, and inverse Gaussian models share a structure. An observable driver \(Z(t)\) accumulates information. Two measures give different probabilities to its increments. Price is the likelihood ratio of those two models.
The driver is additive; the price is multiplicative. “Linear information flow” refers to the affine log likelihood and its expected accumulation, not to a price moving along a straight line.

title: Linear information flow
text:
Add increments, multiply likelihoods
Suppose nonoverlapping increments are independent under each of two consistent process laws. Their densities or mass functions belong to the same time-scaled exponential family:
\[
f(z,t;\theta)=h(z,t)\exp\{\theta z-t\kappa(\theta)\}.
\]
Keep the common base \(h(z,t)\) and any shared shape or variance parameters fixed. Change the natural parameter from \(\theta_Y\) to \(\theta_X\). The base cancels:
\[
\log\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}=aZ(t)+bt,
\]
where the two constants are
\[
a=\theta_X-\theta_Y,
\]
\[
b=-\{\kappa(\theta_X)-\kappa(\theta_Y)\}.
\]
The likelihood ratio of a full sequence of increments has exactly the same form, because their sums are \(Z(t)\) and \(t\). Thus the terminal statistic retains the information needed to compare this particular pair of process models. Independently chosen densities at unrelated horizons would not guarantee such a consistent process.

title: Linear information flow
section: Why the expected information is linear
text:
Why the expected information is linear
If \(\mathbb E^X[Z(t)]=m_Xt\), then the two laws of observations through time \(t\) satisfy
\[
\begin{aligned}
D(\mathbb P^X\Vert\mathbb P^Y)
&=\mathbb E^X\!\left[\log\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}\right]\\
&=k_Xt,
\end{aligned}
\]
with \(k_X=am_X+b\geq0\). Under the market measure the expected log price goes the other way:
\[
\mathbb E^Y\!\left[\log\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}\right]
=-k_Yt,
\]
where \(k_Y\) is the reverse divergence over one unit of time. The two information rates need not be equal. Their signs describe the same position evaluated by two different models.
Prices still satisfy \(\mathbb E^Y[X(t)]=X(0)\). There is no contradiction: the logarithm is concave, so mean wealth and mean log wealth are different quantities.

title: Linear information flow
text:
The six clocks

Binomial time is an integer trial count. Negative-binomial time is an integer failure count; each step contains a random number of trials. Normal, Poisson, gamma, and inverse Gaussian processes can be observed on any positive time grid. Their increment distributions remain in the same family with the appropriate time scaling.

title: Linear information flow
text:
A common scale for comparison
A raw parameter change has different meanings across families. Moving a Poisson intensity by one is not comparable to moving a normal mean by one. The forward KL rate \(k_X\) gives a common information scale: nats per unit of the stated clock.
The continuous-model laboratories therefore start from a chosen \(k_X\), then infer the compatible second parameter. Additional controls change the event rate or shape of the information stream. Two models can have the same information rate and still produce very different paths, downside behavior, and higher moments.
These bounded controls are teaching choices. They are not fitted market parameters or limits imposed by the theory. In particular, fixing forward KL does not fix reverse KL or every tail risk.

title: Linear information flow
text:
What a simulated path shows

Normal: exact Gaussian increments on the chosen grid; joining them visually does not resolve the Brownian motion between grid points.
Poisson: finite event activity; arrivals produce visible price jumps, with deterministic movement between them.
Gamma and inverse Gaussian: infinitely many small jumps in every positive interval. Exact increment sampling gives exact distributions at the grid times; the display does not locate all intervening jumps.

The asset price may have upward or downward jumps depending on the sign of \(a\), even when the information driver only increases. For all families, the likelihood ratio is evaluated without discretizing an SDE. Exact finite-increment simulation is also available in classical models when their transition law is known—the normal/GBM example is a direct instance of that agreement.

title: Linear information flow
text:
Where to go next
Use normal and GBM for the connection with stochastic calculus, Poisson for a visible jump clock, then gamma and inverse Gaussian for infinite activity. The negative-binomial model provides the cleanest comparison of different sampling clocks carrying the same likelihood evidence.
Source: Jan Vecer, Principles of Portfolio Choice, Chapter 5, “Dynamic Price Models with Linear Information Flow.”

title: Relative entropy
text:
Relative entropy answers a specific question: how much log evidence does one probability model expect to accumulate against another? In likelihood finance, exactly the same quantity measures an asset’s expected log return under its own implied measure.
The framework constructs an investment from probabilities. Here we slow down at the information-theoretic step: ratios, logarithms, and the probabilities used to average them.

title: Relative entropy
text:
First compare one observation
Consider two possible outcomes, A and B. The asset measure and the pricing measure assign these probabilities:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb P^X&=(0.6,0.4),\\
\mathbb P^Y&=(0.5,0.5).
\end{aligned}
\]
If A occurs, its likelihood ratio is \(0.6/0.5=1.2\). That observation is 20% more likely under the asset model than under the pricing model. It favors \(\mathbb P^X\) over \(\mathbb P^Y\).
If B occurs, the ratio is \(0.4/0.5=0.8\). That observation favors \(\mathbb P^Y\). A likelihood ratio is a comparison between two specified models; it is not, by itself, a probability that either model is true.

title: Relative entropy
text:
Take logarithms so evidence adds
Independent likelihood ratios multiply. Taking their logarithms turns that multiplication into addition, which makes accumulated evidence easier to track. For our two outcomes,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log(1.2)&\approx+0.1823216,\\
\log(0.8)&\approx-0.2231436.
\end{aligned}
\]
Positive log evidence favors the numerator model; negative log evidence favors the denominator. Notice that the positive and negative values are not equal in magnitude. Multiplying wealth by \(1.2\) and then by \(0.8\) leaves \(0.96\) of the original wealth, so those two moves do not cancel.
We use natural logarithms throughout. Their information unit is the nat. A different logarithm base would rescale every information value; it would not change which model an observation favors.

title: Relative entropy
text:
Average using the first model
Now ask what the asset model expects. Under \(\mathbb P^X\), A has weight \(0.6\) and B has weight \(0.4\). Multiply each log ratio by that probability:
\[
\begin{aligned}
0.6\log(1.2)&\approx+0.109392934,\\
0.4\log(0.8)&\approx-0.089257421.
\end{aligned}
\]
Adding the contributions gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
D(\mathbb P^X\Vert\mathbb P^Y)\\
=0.6\log(1.2)+0.4\log(0.8)\\
\approx0.02013551\text{ nats}.
\end{gathered}
\]
The negative contribution remains part of the calculation. Relative entropy is an average of signed log evidence, not an average of absolute differences.
For any finite set of outcomes, write the two distributions as \(p=(p_i)\) and \(q=(q_i)\). The definition is
\[
D(p\Vert q)=\sum_i p_i\log\frac{p_i}{q_i}.
\]
Read the order carefully: divide first by second; average with first. This is also called Kullback–Leibler divergence, or KL divergence. We use \(D\) and \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}\) for the same quantity.

title: Relative entropy
text:
Try the calculation yourself
In the laboratory, A is called Success and B is called Failure. Move the asset probability first, then the market probability. Watch the individual log returns and their weighted contributions. Finally make the two probabilities equal: each ratio becomes one, every log ratio becomes zero, and relative entropy vanishes.

The interactive laboratory requires JavaScript. Its default example uses asset probabilities \((0.6,0.4)\) and market probabilities \((0.5,0.5)\). The corresponding returns are \((1.2,0.8)\) and the relative entropy is approximately \(0.02013551\) nats.

title: Relative entropy
text:
Why the average is nonnegative
The reason is the concavity of the logarithm: the log of an average is at least the average of the logs. This is Jensen’s inequality.
For the finite-state case, average \(q_i/p_i\) using the weights \(p_i\). Include only states with \(p_i>0\), so no division by zero is needed:
\[
\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\frac{q_i}{p_i}
=\sum_{i:p_i>0}q_i\le1.
\]
Applying Jensen gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
-D(p\Vert q)
&=\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\log\frac{q_i}{p_i}\\
&\le\log\!\left(\sum_{i:p_i>0}q_i\right)\\
&\le0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(D(p\Vert q)\ge0\). Equality requires the ratio \(q_i/p_i\) to be constant on the support of \(p\) and all of \(q\)’s mass to lie there. Since both distributions sum to one, this means \(p=q\). If some \(p_i>0\) but \(q_i=0\), the divergence is infinite, so the inequality still holds.
Individual observations may support either model, but a model expects nonnegative log evidence in its own favor when the averaging uses its probabilities. This does not establish which model describes reality, nor guarantee positive evidence in a particular sample. Even in our example, a run of B outcomes can produce a large loss.
The order generally matters. Reversing our two distributions gives
\[
D(\mathbb P^Y\Vert\mathbb P^X)
\approx0.02041100\text{ nats}.
\]
The ratios are inverted and the averaging probabilities change. KL divergence is therefore asymmetric; it is not an ordinary geometric distance between two points.

title: Relative entropy
section: The financial meaning of the same calculation
text:
The financial meaning of the same calculation
Measure prices in units of a strictly positive traded reference investment, with distributions reinvested, so \(Y(T)=1\) in its own units. A nonnegative asset \(X\) with positive initial price and implied measure \(\mathbb P^X\) has gross return
\[
\frac{X(T)}{X(0)}
=\frac{\mathbb P^X(\omega)}{\mathbb P^Y(\omega)}.
\]
The likelihood ratios \(1.2\) and \(0.8\) are thus also the asset’s two wealth multipliers. Taking logarithms and averaging under \(\mathbb P^X\) gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
\mathbb E^X\!\left[\log\frac{X(T)}{X(0)}\right]\\
=D(\mathbb P^X\Vert\mathbb P^Y).
\end{gathered}
\]
The value \(0.02013551\) is an expected log return. It is not the expected ordinary percentage return. In this example, the expected gross return under \(\mathbb P^X\) is
\[
0.6(1.2)+0.4(0.8)=1.04,
\]
so the expected simple return is 4%. Averaging returns and averaging their logarithms answer different questions.
The superscript on \(\mathbb E^X\) matters just as much as the logarithm. An investor may hold beliefs \(\mathbb P^M\) different from the asset’s implied measure. If that investor assigns probabilities \((0.4,0.6)\) instead, the very same asset has expected log return approximately \(-0.06096\) under her beliefs. The nonnegative divergence identity becomes her expected-performance statement only when \(\mathbb P^M=\mathbb P^X\).

title: Relative entropy
text:
Continuous observations use densities
For a continuous observation, an exact point usually has probability zero under both models. Dividing those point probabilities would give no useful ratio. Instead compare densities with respect to the same underlying variable:
\[
\begin{gathered}
D(f_X\Vert f_Y)\\
=\int f_X(z)\log\frac{f_X(z)}{f_Y(z)}\,dz.
\end{gathered}
\]
This is the same instruction as before: take a density ratio, take its logarithm, and average under the first density. The normal model illustrates it explicitly with two bell-shaped curves and their likelihood-ratio price.

title: Relative entropy
section: From expected performance to long-run growth
text:
From expected performance to long-run growth
Why use expected log performance as a growth criterion? Repeat the same investment independently. Let \(p\) and \(q\) be the per-trial asset and market distributions, and write the gross return in period \(k\) as
\[
G(k)=\frac{p(\omega(k))}{q(\omega(k))}.
\]
Reinvesting the proceeds compounds these returns:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{X(n)}{X(0)}&=\prod_{k=1}^{n}G(k),\\
\log\frac{X(n)}{X(0)}&=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\log G(k).
\end{aligned}
\]
The expected log return after \(n\) periods is \(nD(p\Vert q)\) under the asset model. More is true: if the observations are independent and identically distributed and the one-period log return is integrable, the strong law of large numbers gives
\[
\frac1n\log\frac{X(n)}{X(0)}
\longrightarrow D(p\Vert q)
\]
almost surely under \(\mathbb P^X\). This means convergence on a set of paths with probability one under the asset model. Relative entropy is the long-run log growth rate in this repeated experiment. The statement is conditional on the chosen model governing the observations; it does not establish that the model is correct.

The fair-game paradox
Under the market model, each return has mean one. Nevertheless, Jensen’s inequality gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E^Y[\log G(1)]
&\le\log\mathbb E^Y[G(1)]\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
For distinct positive \(p\) and \(q\), the inequality is strict. Averaging the same log ratios under \(q\) gives \(-D(q\Vert p)\). With the same independence and integrability assumptions, now under the market model,
\[
\frac1n\log\frac{X(n)}{X(0)}
\longrightarrow -D(q\Vert p)
\]
almost surely under \(\mathbb P^Y\). So typical market-model paths decay toward zero even though
\[
\mathbb E^Y[X(n)]=X(0)
\]
at every finite date. Increasingly rare, very large outcomes sustain the arithmetic average. There is no contradiction: average wealth across many possible outcomes and long-run growth along a typical path are different quantities. If \(p=q\), every multiplier is one and there is no growth or decay.
In our example the two long-run log rates are about \(+0.02014\) under the asset model and \(-0.02041\) under the market model. Generate paths in the binomial model to see the distinction. The linear information flow page develops the common additive structure across model families.






NoteMarket averaging, zeros, and support





When both distributions are positive, averaging the same log return under the market measure reverses the divergence:
\[
\begin{gathered}
\mathbb E^Y\!\left[\log\frac{X(T)}{X(0)}\right]\\
=-D(\mathbb P^Y\Vert\mathbb P^X).
\end{gathered}
\]
In the example this is approximately \(-0.02041100\), even though the market’s expected gross return is one.
Throughout the finite-state construction, market state prices satisfy \(q_i>0\). Asset probabilities may be zero: the convention \(0\log(0/q_i)=0\) reflects the limiting value of that expression. If \(p_i=0\) while \(q_i>0\), the asset pays zero in that state. Its expected log return under a model assigning positive probability to that state is \(-\infty\); the corresponding reverse divergence is \(+\infty\). In independent repetitions under the market model, such a state is eventually encountered with probability one, and reinvested wealth then stays at zero. The finite-log-mean assumption for the displayed market strong law does not apply in this case.
For general density models, positive mass under the numerator outside the denominator’s support gives infinite divergence. Finite subtraction identities require suitable support and integrability assumptions; one must not subtract two infinities.



Source: Jan Vecer, Principles of Portfolio Choice: An Information-Theoretic, Likelihood-Based Perspective, Chapters 1–3. Continue to utility and risk aversion to see how an investor’s chosen payoff can differ from the belief-matching investment.

title: Likelihood Finance
text:
Start with a simple question: if you and the market disagree about the chances of an outcome, what investment expresses your view? We will answer it with one bet, work through a football example, and then introduce the mathematics that connects portfolios with information.
This is a web companion to Jan Vecer’s Principles of Portfolio Choice. No knowledge of information theory is needed to begin.

title: Likelihood Finance
section: 1. Choose the unit in which we measure wealth
text:
1. Choose the unit in which we measure wealth
Fix a strictly positive traded reference asset \(Y\), held as a self-financing, total-return investment: any distributions are reinvested, rather than paid out separately. An interest-bearing account is one example. Express every price and payoff in units of \(Y\): how many units of the reference asset could you exchange it for? In these units, the reference asset itself always has value
\[
Y(t)=1.
\]
If \(Y\) is a cash account, this means measuring performance relative to that account. We write \(X(0)\) for another asset’s price now and \(X(T)\) for its value at the final date. The ratio \(X(T)/X(0)\) is its gross return in these reference units.
Begin with finitely many possible outcomes and a market that lets us buy a separate claim on each one. Each quoted state price is strictly positive; trading is frictionless and arbitrage-free. Later we will ask what changes when only a few bundled assets are available.

title: Likelihood Finance
section: 2. Understand one claim before building a portfolio
text:
2. Understand one claim before building a portfolio
Suppose a football team can win, draw, or lose. A win claim pays one unit of \(Y\) if the team wins, and zero otherwise. Suppose it costs \(0.50\) units of \(Y\).
Spending one unit buys two such claims. If the team wins, they pay two units. Thus the claim’s price is \(q=0.5\), while its payout per unit staked—the decimal odds—is
\[
\frac{1}{q}=2.
\]
These are two descriptions of the same contract: price per claim and payout per unit spent.
Buying one claim on every outcome guarantees exactly one unit of \(Y\) at the final date. Holding one unit of the reference investment delivers the same thing. By the law of one price, the claims together cost one unit of \(Y\) now, so their prices sum to one.1 We denote this distribution of market state prices by \(\mathbb P^Y\). It is a pricing distribution; it need not agree with an investor’s assessment of the chances.

3. Turn your probabilities into stakes
Suppose you have \(1{,}000\) units to invest. You assign probabilities \(0.6\), \(0.3\), and \(0.1\) to Win, Draw, and Loss. Call your belief distribution \(\mathbb P^M\).
Allocate your budget in those proportions: \(600\) to Win, \(300\) to Draw, and \(100\) to Loss. To find the number of claims bought, divide each stake by the corresponding claim price.

If Win occurs, only the win claims pay, so your final wealth is \(1{,}200\). If Draw occurs, it is \(1{,}000\); if Loss occurs, it is \(500\). The three final wealth values are alternatives, not amounts to add together.
Write \(M\) for this investment. In outcome \(\omega\), its stake is \(M(0)\mathbb P^M(\omega)\). Dividing by the price per claim gives
\[
M(T,\omega)
=\frac{M(0)\mathbb P^M(\omega)}{\mathbb P^Y(\omega)}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\frac{M(T,\omega)}{M(0)}
=\frac{\mathbb P^M(\omega)}{\mathbb P^Y(\omega)}.
\]
This ratio of probabilities is a likelihood ratio. The win return is \(0.6/0.5=1.2\): your model puts more weight on Win than the market does, and your position pays more if Win occurs. Nothing has yet been optimized; we have simply translated probabilities into an investment.

title: Likelihood Finance
text:
4. Run the construction backwards
A payoff can also be translated into a probability distribution. Suppose a different investment \(V\) costs \(1{,}000\) and pays \((800,1200,1200)\) in the same three outcomes. Its price is consistent with the market weights because
\[
\begin{aligned}
&0.5(800)+0.3(1200)\\
&\quad+0.2(1200)=1000.
\end{aligned}
\]
Divide its payoffs by its cost to obtain the returns \((0.8,1.2,1.2)\). Multiply those returns by the market probabilities:
\[
\mathbb P^V=(0.4,0.36,0.24).
\]
The entries sum to one. This is the distribution implied by the payoff, whether or not its owner consciously selected those probabilities. In general,
\[
\mathbb P^V(\omega)
=\frac{V(T,\omega)}{V(0)}\mathbb P^Y(\omega).
\]
The budget fixes the size of the investment; this distribution describes how its payoff is spread across outcomes. We can move in either direction: probabilities determine a payoff, and a fairly priced nonnegative payoff determines probabilities.

title: Likelihood Finance
text:
5. Measure the football investment’s performance
The football investment \(M\) has wealth multipliers \(1.2\), \(1\), and \(0.5\). A multiplier of \(1.2\) means a 20% gain; \(0.5\) means a 50% loss. Their log returns are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log(1.2)&\approx0.1823,\\
\log(1)&=0,\\
\log(0.5)&\approx-0.6931.
\end{aligned}
\]
Why logarithms? Successive wealth multipliers multiply, while their logarithms add. In repeated independent investments, average log performance approaches expected log performance, provided the log return is integrable. This makes it a measure of long-run compounded growth. We derive that connection on the relative-entropy page.
An expectation must specify which probabilities do the averaging. Start with your beliefs, \((0.6,0.3,0.1)\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E^M\!\left[\log\frac{M(T)}{M(0)}\right]\\
&=0.6\log(1.2)+0.3\log(1)\\
&\quad+0.1\log(0.5)\\
&\approx0.0401.
\end{aligned}
\]
Now use the market weights, \((0.5,0.3,0.2)\), to average the same three log returns:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E^Y\!\left[\log\frac{M(T)}{M(0)}\right]\\
&=0.5\log(1.2)+0.3\log(1)\\
&\quad+0.2\log(0.5)\\
&\approx-0.0475.
\end{aligned}
\]
The market assigns twice as much weight to the loss. The investment therefore has positive expected log performance under your beliefs and negative expected log performance under the market weights. Neither average guarantees a particular outcome.

Those averages have an information interpretation
Recall that each wealth multiplier is a ratio of probabilities. For two distributions \(p\) and \(q\) on the same outcomes, define
\[
D(p\Vert q)
=\sum_i p_i\log\frac{p_i}{q_i}.
\]
For each outcome, divide its two probabilities, take the logarithm, and then average using the first distribution, \(p\). This is relative entropy, also called Kullback–Leibler divergence. Natural logarithms give units called nats.
Our first calculation is exactly this definition:
\[
D(\mathbb P^M\Vert\mathbb P^Y)\approx0.0401.
\]
For the market average, reverse the order of the distributions and change the sign:
\[
-D(\mathbb P^Y\Vert\mathbb P^M)\approx-0.0475.
\]
Here “information” means average log evidence distinguishing two models. A likelihood ratio above one favors the numerator model; a ratio below one favors the denominator. Relative entropy averages that log evidence under the numerator model. It is nonnegative and vanishes only when the distributions agree. The relative-entropy page explains why and lets you examine each contribution.

Every asset has the same information identity
Any fairly priced nonnegative asset \(X\) of positive cost has its own implied measure \(\mathbb P^X\), just as \(V\) does in Section 4. The same identity holds with \(X\) in place of \(M\):
\[
\begin{gathered}
\mathbb E^X\!\left[\log\frac{X(T)}{X(0)}\right]\\
=\mathbb E^X\!\left[\log\frac{d\mathbb P^X}{d\mathbb P^Y}\right]\\
=D(\mathbb P^X\Vert\mathbb P^Y).
\end{gathered}
\]
In our finite example, \(d\mathbb P^X/d\mathbb P^Y\) is simply the state-by-state probability ratio. The expectation is under \(\mathbb P^X\), the same measure as the numerator. This measure describes the asset’s payoff; it need not equal your personal belief \(\mathbb P^M\). The football investment matched those beliefs because we deliberately constructed it that way.

title: Likelihood Finance
section: 7. What if your payoff expresses a different model?
text:
7. What if your payoff expresses a different model?
Your beliefs can stay at \(\mathbb P^M\) while you choose a payoff with implied distribution \(\mathbb P^V\). Let \(G(T)=V(T)/V(0)\) be its gross return. The expected log return now decomposes as
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E^M[\log G(T)]
&=D(\mathbb P^M\Vert\mathbb P^Y)\\
&\quad-D(\mathbb P^M\Vert\mathbb P^V).
\end{aligned}
\]
Read it in two steps. The first term is the information in your beliefs relative to market prices. The second is the mismatch between your beliefs and the distribution your payoff implements. Subtracting it gives your expected log performance.
Because relative entropy is nonnegative, that mismatch cannot improve expected log growth under your beliefs. Choosing \(\mathbb P^V=\mathbb P^M\) removes it. This is why the original investment \(M\) is log-optimal when all state claims are available: the optimality follows from the construction.

NoteSupport, zero payoffs, and attainability





Beliefs and payoffs may contain zeros. If the investor assigns positive probability to a zero-payoff state, expected log growth is \(-\infty\), and the mismatch is \(+\infty\). The finite-market identity remains valid in this extended sense.
For general scenario spaces, use densities and require \(\mathbb P^M\ll\mathbb P^Y\) and \(D(\mathbb P^M\Vert\mathbb P^Y)<\infty\) for the displayed subtraction. This avoids an undefined difference of infinities.
The payoff-to-measure map requires only fair pricing and a nonnegative payoff of positive finite cost. Implementing every desired measure additionally requires a rich enough asset menu. title: Likelihood Finance
text:
From distributions to price processes
A traded asset has a measure \(\mathbb P^X\), which need not equal any investor’s beliefs. Its relative price is the likelihood ratio \(\mathbb P^X/\mathbb P^Y\) on the information observed so far. Classical martingale pricing and this construction are compatible; they start from different primitives.
The likelihood and dynamics page states the fundamental theorem of asset pricing and compares the two directions. The linear information flow page gives the common structure behind all six families.


Binomial
Two outcomes per trial. Recover both measures from the two martingale conditions.


Negative binomial
The same trials, counted until a fixed number of failures. A new clock, the same likelihood evidence.


Normal
Continuous information. Derive geometric Brownian motion directly from two normal densities.


Poisson
Information arrives as countable events. Compare event rates and generate jump paths.


Gamma
Positive increments of many sizes. Keep the shape clock fixed and compare rates.


Inverse Gaussian
A first-passage interpretation and an alternative pattern of positive jump activity.


Each family has explicit prices and linear expected information accumulation. The continuous-model laboratories let you choose a bounded KL rate and an event or shape parameter, then generate paths under both measures. The displayed ranges keep the examples readable; they are illustrative calibrations.

NoteA further connection: statistical testing





The market measure \(\mathbb P^Y\) can serve as a null model, and an asset or portfolio measure as an alternative. A fairly priced, normalized, nonnegative payoff is an e-value: its expectation under the null is one. Consistent likelihood ratios through time form a nonnegative martingale. Ville’s inequality then controls the chance, under the null, of ever crossing a chosen evidence threshold. Explore it in the binomial model.



Kelly (1956) connected information rate and capital growth; Cover and Thomas give the finite horse-race identity. Geman, El Karoui, and Rochet developed the change-of-numeraire relation between traded assets and probability measures. This site uses these connections as a common language for pricing and portfolio choice.

title: Two ways to build a market
text:
The classical approach starts with asset prices and asks which probability measure makes their discounted evolution a martingale. The likelihood approach can start with the measures and obtain the price moves from their ratios. The mathematical connection is exact. What changes is the choice of inputs.
All prices below are in units of a strictly positive reference asset \(Y\). Thus \(Y\) itself has constant value one.

title: Two ways to build a market
text:
Start with the dynamics
Specify a finite set of possible states, a finite trading horizon, and the prices and payoffs of the traded assets. Assume frictionless trading, unrestricted borrowing and short selling, no intermediate dividends, and that every state is possible. An arbitrage is a self-financing strategy with zero initial cost, nonnegative terminal payoff in every state, and a positive payoff in at least one state.
The fundamental theorem of asset pricing, in this finite, discrete setting, says:






NoteExistence: no arbitrage



There is no arbitrage if and only if there exists a probability measure \(\mathbb P^Y\), positive on every possible state, under which every traded price in units of \(Y\) is a martingale.


For a one-period asset with gross returns \(R_i\) this gives two equations:
\[
\sum_i q_i=1,
\qquad
\sum_i q_i R_i=1,
\]
where \(q_i=\mathbb P^Y(\omega_i)>0\). Over several periods the pricing equation becomes conditional:
\[
\mathbb E^Y[X(t+1)\mid\mathcal F_t]=X(t).
\]
These equations identify a pricing measure when their solution is unique. Otherwise, they identify a family of admissible measures. The investor’s subjective probabilities \(\mathbb P^M\) need not be the pricing probabilities.






NoteUniqueness: completeness



In the same finite, arbitrage-free setting, the market is complete if and only if its equivalent martingale measure is unique. Completeness means that trading the available assets can replicate every terminal payoff.


No arbitrage ensures that a consistent pricing rule exists. Completeness is the additional property that makes every contingent payoff replicable and its price unique. Portfolio constraints can further restrict what an investor can implement.

title: Two ways to build a market
section: Now read the same market through likelihoods
text:
Now read the same market through likelihoods
Fix a pricing measure \(\mathbb P^Y\) and a strictly positive traded asset \(X\). At the terminal date define
\[
\mathbb P^X(\omega)
=\frac{X(T,\omega)}{X(0)}\,\mathbb P^Y(\omega).
\]
The martingale pricing equation says exactly that these weights sum to one. Rearranging gives
\[
\frac{X(T,\omega)}{X(0)}
=\frac{\mathbb P^X(\omega)}{\mathbb P^Y(\omega)}.
\]
Conversely, specify two positive probability distributions. Their ratio defines a unit-cost return whose expectation under \(\mathbb P^Y\) is one. For a process, use their consistent restrictions to the information available at each date:
\[
\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}
=\left.\frac{d\mathbb P^X}{d\mathbb P^Y}\right|_{\mathcal F_t}.
\]
The conditional likelihood ratio is a \(\mathbb P^Y\)-martingale. Positive prices also permit the reverse direction:
\[
\frac{X(0)}{X(t)}
=\left.\frac{d\mathbb P^Y}{d\mathbb P^X}\right|_{\mathcal F_t},
\]
which is a martingale under \(\mathbb P^X\). In financial terms, the price of \(Y\) in units of \(X\) is fair under the \(X\)-numeraire measure, just as the price of \(X\) in units of \(Y\) is fair under the \(Y\)-numeraire measure.

title: Two ways to build a market
text:
Two states identify the measure
For the nondegenerate binomial model, assume \(u>1>d>0\). The pricing equation is
\[
qu+(1-q)d=1.
\]
There is a unique solution:
\[
q=\frac{1-d}{u-d},
\qquad p=uq.
\]
Starting from \(p\) and \(q\) instead recovers the same moves:
\[
u=\frac pq,
\qquad d=\frac{1-p}{1-q}.
\]
With two states and two independent traded payoffs, the stock and the reference asset span every payoff. This is why the pricing measure is unique. If both returns equal one, that independence is lost; the market cannot distinguish the two states through these assets.

section: Three states reveal what is missing
text:
Three states reveal what is missing
Add a middle state while keeping only the stock and the reference asset. For the book’s returns
\[
R=\left(\frac32,1,\frac12\right),
\]
all the following measures price the same stock:
\[
\mathbb P^Y=(t,1-2t,t),
\qquad 0<t<\frac12.
\]
For each such choice, the associated asset measure is
\[
\mathbb P^X
=\left(\frac{3t}{2},1-2t,\frac t2\right).
\]
The return vector alone does not select \(t\). Another traded claim, a calibration target, or an explicit modeling criterion can supply additional information.
Choosing the measures directly makes the pricing identities automatic. It does not make the measures observable or make missing payoffs tradable. A model still needs a way to select its inputs, and portfolio choice still takes place within the span of the available assets.

title: The binomial model
text:
Each period has two scenarios, success and failure. The market prices success at \(q=\mathbb P^Y(\text{success})\). A traded asset \(X\) carries its own measure, with \(p=\mathbb P^X(\text{success})\). The investor’s model \(\mathbb P^M\) is a third object: the asset \(X\) is her log-optimal holding only when \(\mathbb P^M=\mathbb P^X\). Every identity on the framework page has an explicit two-state form, and repeating the period turns them into a price process. All prices and returns below are in units of the reference asset \(Y\).
This is the first worked example of likelihoods and price dynamics: the two approaches describe the same market, but start with different primitives.

title: The binomial model
text:
Two probabilities, two multipliers
Take \(p,q\in(0,1)\). Likelihood-ratio pricing, \(X(1)/X(0)=\mathbb P^X/\mathbb P^Y\), gives the success and failure multipliers directly (up and down, respectively, when \(p>q\)):
\[
\begin{aligned}
u&=\frac{p}{q},\\
d&=\frac{1-p}{1-q}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The corresponding asset return is
\[
\frac{X(1)}{X(0)}=
\begin{cases} u & \text{success},\\ d & \text{failure}.\end{cases}
\]
There are two martingale conditions, one for each choice of numeraire. Under the reference-asset measure \(\mathbb P^Y\), the normalized price of \(X\) has expectation one:
\[
\begin{aligned}
q\,u+(1-q)\,d
&=p+(1-p)\\
&=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Under the asset measure \(\mathbb P^X\), the normalized price of \(Y\) in units of \(X\) is the reciprocal return. It also has expectation one:
\[
\begin{aligned}
p\,\frac1u+(1-p)\,\frac1d
&=q+(1-q)\\
&=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
The first condition identifies \(q\) from nonconstant price multipliers; the second identifies \(p\). Thus \(p\) is the probability associated with the asset numeraire, not an independently supplied forecast of the success frequency. The investor’s forecast is \(p^M\).
The classical one-period model runs the other way. It postulates \(u\) and \(d\) and derives the pricing probabilities from these martingale conditions. Solving them gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
q&=\frac{1-d}{u-d},\\
p&=\frac{u(1-d)}{u-d}=u\,q.
\end{aligned}
\]
The map \((p,q)\mapsto(u,d)\) sends \(\{0<q<p<1\}\) one-to-one onto \(\{0<d<1<u\}\). Read backwards, the classical no-arbitrage condition \(d<1<u\) corresponds to two interior probabilities ordered so that success is the up move. With \(p<q\), success is the down move and \(0<u<1<d\). When \(p=q\), \(u=d=1\): the asset has the reference asset’s return. In that degenerate case the return identifies neither probability, and the inverse formulas are undefined. Equal multipliers different from one imply deterministic arbitrage in units of \(Y\), under the frictionless borrowing and short-selling assumptions.
With two states, cash and a nonconstant asset span all payoffs, which is why these conditions identify the two measures uniquely. The trinomial model shows what changes when there are three states and only two traded assets.

Both numeraire martingale conditions appear below the diagram. Multipliers on the same side of 1, or one equal to 1 and the other different, imply arbitrage when both scenarios are possible. title: The binomial model
text:
Every position on one curve
Write \(d(a\Vert b)\) for the relative entropy between Bernoulli laws with probabilities \(a\) and \(b\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
d(a\Vert b)
&=a\log\frac ab\\
&\quad +(1-a)\log\frac{1-a}{1-b}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The usual conventions apply: a zero-probability term contributes zero, while positive probability divided by zero gives infinite divergence.
Let the investor’s model be \(\mathbb P^M(\text{success})=p^M\). With two scenarios a nonnegative portfolio \(V\) of positive price is determined, up to scale, by \(v=\mathbb P^V(\text{success})\), the fraction of wealth spent on the success claim. Its expected log return under the investor’s model is
\[
\begin{aligned}
g(v)
&=p^M\log\frac{v}{q}\\
&\quad +(1-p^M)\log\frac{1-v}{1-q}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The information decomposition becomes
\[
g(v)=d(p^M\Vert q)-d(p^M\Vert v).
\]
Three points on the curve have names. At \(v=q\) the investor holds the reference asset and \(g=0\). At \(v=p\) she holds the asset \(X\). At \(v=p^M\) the curve peaks at \(d(p^M\Vert q)\), and the shortfall of any other position is exactly \(d(p^M\Vert v)\). Every portfolio is log-optimal for the model it implies, and for no other in this unconstrained two-state market.
For \(\gamma\ge1\), risk aversion moves the position from \(p^M\) back toward \(q\), in one of two ways. Fractional Kelly keeps a cash reserve:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f&=1/\gamma,\\
v_f&=(1-f)\,q+f\,p^M.
\end{aligned}
\]
CRRA utility instead tempers the measure. Set \(\alpha=1/\gamma\) and form the weights
\[
\begin{aligned}
w_s&=(p^M)^\alpha q^{1-\alpha},\\
w_f&=(1-p^M)^\alpha(1-q)^{1-\alpha}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The optimal success weight is
\[
v_\gamma=\frac{w_s}{w_s+w_f}.
\]
For \(0<p^M<1\) both families sweep the same segment between \(q\) and \(p^M\), including cash as a limit as \(\gamma\to\infty\). They generally traverse it at different rates: the same numerical \(\gamma\) can give different positions, while a change of \(\gamma\) can match them. With three or more states they generally trace different curves in the simplex, arithmetic against normalized geometric interpolation. Boundary beliefs give another distinction: set \(\mathbb P^M(\text{success})=0\) in the figure. For every finite \(\gamma\), CRRA keeps that zero, while fractional Kelly with \(\gamma>1\) assigns positive weight through its cash reserve. The utility and risk-aversion page develops the general construction.

The separate marker lanes below the curve keep all six positions identifiable even when they coincide; vertical leaders connect the lane markers to their positions on the curve. The ring and diamond denote fractional Kelly and CRRA at the chosen \(\gamma\). The key reports each position and its growth numerically.

title: The binomial model
text:
Many periods
Repeat the period independently and let \(S(n)\) count the successes after \(n\) periods. Likelihood-ratio pricing at time \(n\) gives
\[
\frac{X(n)}{X(0)}
=\Big(\frac pq\Big)^{S(n)}
\Big(\frac{1-p}{1-q}\Big)^{n-S(n)}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\frac{X(n)}{X(0)}=u^{S(n)}d^{\,n-S(n)}.
\]
The binomial coefficients in \(\mathbb P^X\) and \(\mathbb P^Y\) cancel. The price depends on the path only through the sufficient statistic \(S(n)\), and its logarithm is affine in it:
\[
\log\frac{X(n)}{X(0)}=a\,S(n)+b\,n.
\]
Here the coefficients are
\[
\begin{aligned}
a&=\log(u/d),\\
b&=\log d.
\end{aligned}
\]
Write \(D^{X,Y}(n)\) for the divergence between the laws of \(S(n)\) under the two measures. Independence gives
\[
D^{X,Y}(n)=n\,d(p\Vert q).
\]
This is linear information flow. The binomial tree is the first of the price models in Chapter 5, not a separate construction.
Under \(\mathbb P^Y\) the price \(X(t)/X(0)\) is a nonnegative martingale with mean one. Ville’s inequality then gives, for every horizon \(n\),
\[
\mathbb P^Y\Big(\max_{t\le n}\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}\ge\frac1\alpha\Big)\le\alpha .
\]
For \(0<\alpha<1\), the price path of \(X\) is therefore an anytime-valid test of the market’s model against the asset’s: one may stop the moment \(X\) has multiplied by \(1/\alpha\), and the probability of ever crossing under \(\mathbb P^Y\) is at most \(\alpha\). If \(p\ne q\), then under \(\mathbb P^X\) the long-run log growth is the strictly positive one-period divergence, so the threshold is eventually crossed with probability one over an unbounded horizon. If \(p=q\), wealth stays constant and no such rejection occurs.

The outlines remain visible when the laws coincide. Bottom: eight simulated paths under each measure, with the expected log price as dashed lines and the rejection threshold \(\log(1/\alpha)\). Changing \(p\) or \(q\) reuses the same random numbers, so the paths deform rather than redraw.
