title: The negative binomial model
text:
In the binomial model, time counts trials. Here it counts completed failure blocks: observe successive Bernoulli trials and stop a block at its first failure. Count the successes in each block, then add them.
The information driver changes, while the rule stays the same: two probability laws determine a price through their likelihood ratio.

title: The negative binomial model
text:
A different count
Let \(G(j)\) be the number of successes before the failure ending block \(j\). The blocks are independent. Under \(\mathbb P^X\), each trial succeeds with probability \(p\in(0,1)\); under \(\mathbb P^Y\), it succeeds with probability \(q\in(0,1)\).
After \(n\) completed blocks,
\[
Z(n)=G(1)+\cdots+G(n).
\]
This counts successes before the \(n\)-th failure. The book uses the convention
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb P^X(Z(n)=k)\\
&\quad=\binom{n+k-1}{k}(1-p)^n p^k,
\end{aligned}
\]
for \(k=0,1,\ldots\), and the same formula with \(q\) under \(\mathbb P^Y\). We write these laws as \(\mathrm{NB}(n,p)\) and \(\mathrm{NB}(n,q)\). Unlike the binomial count, \(Z(n)\) has no upper bound.

title: The negative binomial model
section: The likelihood ratio is the price
text:
The likelihood ratio is the price
The combinatorial factor cancels between the two laws. Therefore
\[
\frac{X(n)}{X(0)}
=\left(\frac pq\right)^{Z(n)}
\left(\frac{1-p}{1-q}\right)^n.
\]
The logarithm is affine in the accumulated count and the number of completed blocks:
\[
\log\frac{X(n)}{X(0)}=aZ(n)+bn,
\]
\[
a=\log\frac pq,
\qquad b=\log\frac{1-p}{1-q}.
\]
One block can contain any nonnegative number of successes. Its price multiplier is \((p/q)^{G(j)}(1-p)/(1-q)\), whose expectation under \(\mathbb P^Y\) is one. Products over independent blocks therefore form a positive \(\mathbb P^Y\)-martingale; their reciprocals form a \(\mathbb P^X\)-martingale.

The interactive figure requires JavaScript. For \(p=0.60\), \(q=0.40\), the information per completed failure block is approximately \(0.20273\) nats, so after ten blocks the expected log return under \(\mathbb P^X\) is approximately \(2.02733\).

The distributions are shown on the same success-count axis. Their probabilities are not renormalized when the chart truncates the infinite tail. The simulation displays the price itself, starting from \(X(0)=1\), and the logarithms of exactly the same six paths under each measure. Paths are sampled at completed blocks; the individual trials inside a block are not shown. The count-to-price figure can also switch to log price.
The horizontal dashed line in the price figure is \(\mathbb E^Y[X(n)/X(0)]=1\). In the log figure the dashed lines show expected log prices. Exponentiating an expected log price does not give an expected price: rare large outcomes can keep the mean price at one even while most simulated market-measure paths decline. Extremely large prices are explicitly marked as off scale; the log figure retains their full range.

title: The negative binomial model
section: Information grows linearly in block time
text:
Information grows linearly in block time
Let \(D(n;p\Vert q)\) denote the divergence from \(\mathrm{NB}(n,p)\) to \(\mathrm{NB}(n,q)\). Since \(\mathbb E^X[Z(n)]=np/(1-p)\), expected log growth is
\[
\mathbb E^X\left[\log\frac{X(n)}{X(0)}\right]
=D(n;p\Vert q).
\]
Define information per failure block by
\[
I(p,q)=\frac{p}{1-p}\log\frac pq
+\log\frac{1-p}{1-q}.
\]
Then the entire horizon contributes exactly \(nI(p,q)\). This is linear information flow in the book’s clock. It is also the additivity of relative entropy across the independent geometric blocks; their sum \(Z(n)\) retains the likelihood ratio.
Under the pricing measure the direction reverses:
\[
\mathbb E^Y\left[\log\frac{X(n)}{X(0)}\right]
=-nI(q,p).
\]
When \(p=q\), both information rates are zero and the asset has the reference asset’s constant return.

title: The negative binomial model
section: The binomial connection: same observations, same likelihood
text:
The binomial connection: same observations, same likelihood
Suppose the realized data contain \(k\) successes and \(n\) failures. They could have come from an experiment with a fixed total of \(k+n\) trials, or from an experiment stopped at the \(n\)-th failure. For an unknown success probability \(\rho\), both likelihoods are proportional to
\[
L(\rho)\propto\rho^k(1-\rho)^n.
\]
Their proportionality factor depends on the sampling design and the observed counts, but not on \(\rho\). Thus comparing \(p\) with \(q\) gives the same likelihood ratio in either experiment. This illustrates the likelihood principle: proportional likelihood functions carry the same likelihood-based evidence about the parameter.
The sampling distributions differ, so procedures that depend on unobserved outcomes, including conventional fixed-design p-values, can differ. The principle concerns the evidential content of the observed likelihood; it does not say that the two experiments have identical sampling properties.
In financial terms, evaluate the binomial wealth process at the trial when the \(n\)-th failure occurs. Its wealth agrees with the negative-binomial formula above. Here the negative-binomial index \(n\) counts failures, not total trials.

title: The negative binomial model
section: Wald’s identity explains the change of clock
text:
Wald’s identity explains the change of clock
Let \(\tau(n)=Z(n)+n\) be the total number of trials needed for \(n\) failures. Under \(\mathbb P^X\),
\[
\mathbb E^X[\tau(n)]=\frac{n}{1-p}.
\]
The same entropy can be written as
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathrm{NB}(n,p)\Vert\mathrm{NB}(n,q))
\]
\[
=\frac{n}{1-p}\,
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathrm{Bern}(p)\Vert\mathrm{Bern}(q)).
\]
For these bounded one-trial log-likelihood increments and the integrable stopping time \(\tau(n)\), Wald’s identity says: expected accumulated information equals information per trial times the expected number of trials. There is no extra information created by the new clock.






TipRead alongside the book



Jan Vecer, Principles of Portfolio Choice: An Information-Theoretic, Likelihood-Based Perspective, Chapter 5, “Negative binomial family.” The likelihood-principle connection is discussed by D. V. Lindley and L. D. Phillips (1976), “Inference for a Bernoulli Process (A Bayesian View),” The American Statistician 30(3), 112–119. For the stopped-sum identity, see A. Wald (1947), Sequential Analysis.

title: Poisson: events become price jumps
text: In the normal model, the observation is a continuous return driver. Here it is an event count. The pricing measure and the asset measure attach different probabilities to the same sequence of arrivals; their likelihood ratio determines how the price responds to each arrival.

title: Poisson: events become price jumps
text:
Two arrival rates
Let \(N(t)\) count events. Under measure \(\mathbb P^j\), for \(j\in\{X,Y\}\), use a Poisson process with intensity \(\lambda_j>0\):
\[
N(t)\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_jt).
\]
The mass assigned to \(n\) events is
\[
f_j(n,t)=e^{-\lambda_jt}\frac{(\lambda_jt)^n}{n!}.
\]
The factorial and the common power of \(t\) cancel when the two masses are divided:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}
&=\left(\frac{\lambda_X}{\lambda_Y}\right)^{N(t)}
e^{(\lambda_Y-\lambda_X)t},\\
\log\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}&=aN(t)+bt,
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
a=\log\frac{\lambda_X}{\lambda_Y},
\qquad b=\lambda_Y-\lambda_X.
\]
This is again linear information flow. The count is sufficient for the likelihood ratio: with constant intensities, the precise arrival times carry no further likelihood information once the horizon and total count are known.

title: Poisson: events become price jumps
section: Explore arrival frequency and price response
text:
Explore arrival frequency and price response
Choose a pricing intensity, an information rate and a jump direction. The figure solves for \(\lambda_X\) from those choices. The intensity ratio, and hence the size of a price jump, is derived rather than chosen independently.

The interactive model requires JavaScript. Its default pricing intensity is \(\lambda_Y=3\) and the information rate is \(k=0.05\) nats per time unit; the asset intensity is chosen on the downward-jump branch.

title: Poisson: events become price jumps
section: Read the path from the two rates
text:
Read the path from the two rates
At an arrival, \(N\) increases by one and the price is multiplied by
\[
\frac{X(t)}{X(t-)}=\frac{\lambda_X}{\lambda_Y}.
\]
Between arrivals, log price changes at the deterministic rate \(b=\lambda_Y-\lambda_X\).



Rate comparison
At an event
Between events




\(\lambda_X>\lambda_Y\)
Price jumps up.
Price drifts down.


\(\lambda_X<\lambda_Y\)
Price jumps down.
Price drifts up.


\(\lambda_X=\lambda_Y\)
No price response.
Price is constant.



An event that the asset measure regards as more likely than the pricing measure favors the asset measure, so its likelihood-ratio price rises. The drift compensates for this jump response and preserves the pricing-measure martingale identity.
If a local dynamics description is useful, the same process satisfies
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dX(t)}{X(t-)}
&=(r-1)\{dN(t)-\lambda_Ydt\},\\
r&=\frac{\lambda_X}{\lambda_Y}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Under \(\mathbb P^Y\), the expression in braces is a compensated Poisson increment. This equation is a consequence of the likelihood specification.

title: Poisson: events become price jumps
section: The two information rates need not match

title: Poisson: events become price jumps
text:
Exact at every horizon
Independent counts add: Poisson laws with means \(\lambda_js\) and \(\lambda_jt\) sum to a Poisson law with mean \(\lambda_j(s+t)\). The same model therefore works at daily, hourly or finer horizons. In the figure, exponential waiting times produce actual arrival times and the finite sequence of jumps, with the exact drift between them.
Continue: the gamma model replaces a count of isolated events with accumulated positive activity, generated by infinitely many small jumps.






NoteSource and conventions





Jan Vecer, Principles of Portfolio Choice: An Information-Theoretic, Likelihood-Based Perspective, Chapter 5, “Poisson family (counting driver).” The price is measured in units of \(Y\). The asset measure \(\mathbb P^X\) is a subjective investor model only when the investor chooses \(\mathbb P^M=\mathbb P^X\).

title: Inverse Gaussian: a random clock
text:
The inverse Gaussian family supplies a second nonnegative additive driver alongside the gamma model. Its increments have a continuous, right-skewed density, while its paths increase through infinitely many jumps.
One interpretation comes from first-passage times. Let a Brownian motion with positive drift \(\gamma\) run until it first reaches height \(\delta t\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
B(s)&=W(s)+\gamma s,\\
I(t)&=\inf\{s\ge0:B(s)\ge\delta t\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
As the target height increases, the required waiting time forms an inverse Gaussian clock. Here \(t\) indexes the target level; \(s\) is the underlying Brownian clock. The likelihood model can be specified directly through the resulting distributions, without simulating that Brownian first-passage construction.

title: Inverse Gaussian: a random clock
section: Fix the additive scale; vary the tail parameter
text:
Fix the additive scale; vary the tail parameter
Use a common \(\delta>0\) and two positive parameters \(\gamma_X,\gamma_Y\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
I(t)&\sim\operatorname{IG}(\delta t,\gamma_X)
&&\text{under }\mathbb P^X,\\
I(t)&\sim\operatorname{IG}(\delta t,\gamma_Y)
&&\text{under }\mathbb P^Y.
\end{aligned}
\]
In this parameterization, for \(z>0\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_j(z,t)
&=\frac{\delta t}{\sqrt{2\pi}}z^{-3/2}e^{\delta\gamma_jt}\\
&\quad\times\exp\!\left\{
-\frac{\delta^2t^2}{2z}
-\frac{\gamma_j^2z}{2}\right\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The moments help interpret the parameters:
\[
E^j[I(t)]=\frac{\delta t}{\gamma_j},
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}^j[I(t)]=\frac{\delta t}{\gamma_j^3}.
\]
Increasing \(\gamma_j\) reduces both the mean accumulation rate and its variance. Increasing the common scale \(\delta\) increases both linearly.

title: Inverse Gaussian: a random clock
section: A complicated density, a simple ratio
text:
A complicated density, a simple ratio
The common prefactor and the term involving \(1/z\) cancel in the ratio. Only an affine expression remains:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}&=aI(t)+bt,\\
a&=-\frac12(\gamma_X^2-\gamma_Y^2),\\
b&=\delta(\gamma_X-\gamma_Y).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}=\exp\{aI(t)+bt\}.
\]
The common scale \(\delta\) is what removes the nonlinear \(1/I(t)\) term. It is part of the model specification, not an accidental cancellation.

title: Inverse Gaussian: a random clock
section: Explore the clock and its price
text:
Explore the clock and its price
The figure fixes \(\gamma_Y=2\). Choose \(\delta\), the information rate and a price-jump direction; the matching \(\gamma_X\) follows from the KL formula. No drift or jump-size parameter is independently added after the densities have been selected.

The interactive model requires JavaScript. The default common scale is \(\delta=2\), the pricing parameter is \(\gamma_Y=2\) and the forward information rate is \(k=0.05\) nats per time unit.

title: Inverse Gaussian: a random clock
Inverse Gaussian: a random clock
section: What the grid shows—and what it cannot
text:
What the grid shows—and what it cannot
Under \(\mathbb P^j\), the jump intensity density is
\[
\nu_j(dz)=\frac{\delta}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
z^{-3/2}e^{-\gamma_j^2z/2}\,dz.
\]
The \(z^{-3/2}\) singularity is stronger than the gamma model’s \(z^{-1}\) singularity. Both produce infinitely many small jumps and finite total accumulated jump size on bounded time intervals.
Independent increments preserve the family: scales add while \(\gamma_j\) stays fixed. The widget samples the exact law \(\operatorname{IG}(\delta\Delta t,\gamma_j)\) at each grid interval. Its connecting segments visualize observed values and do not resolve the full infinite-activity path. Apparent smoothness at one plotting scale is not evidence of a diffusion.

title: Inverse Gaussian: a random clock
section: One construction, several forms of uncertainty
text:
One construction, several forms of uncertainty
Normal, Poisson, gamma and inverse Gaussian models all produce
\[
\log\frac{X(t)}{X(0)}=aZ(t)+bt.
\]
Their differences lie in the additive observation \(Z(t)\) and in the two laws assigned to it. The likelihood ratio handles the price normalization in every case. Independent drivers can later be combined by multiplying likelihood ratios, so their log prices and divergences add at the level of the joint observation.
Continue: return to linear information flow to compare the families, or to the framework to connect prices with portfolio choice.






NoteSource and conventions





Jan Vecer, Principles of Portfolio Choice: An Information-Theoretic, Likelihood-Based Perspective, Chapter 5, “Inverse Gaussian family.” The book’s \(\operatorname{IG}(\delta t,\gamma)\) convention corresponds to the usual mean–shape parameters \(\mu=\delta t/\gamma\) and \(\lambda=(\delta t)^2\). Prices are in units of \(Y\).

title: Mean–variance & information
text:
Mean–variance analysis describes a portfolio through its expected return and a quadratic measure of risk. Likelihood finance describes its whole payoff through an implied distribution. The connection becomes precise once we specify which measure supplies the quadratic penalty.
Use \(G=V(T)/V(0)\) for a gross payoff and \(Z=G-1\) for its excess return, all in units of \(Y\). Fair pricing means \(\mathbb E^Y[G]=1\), hence \(\mathbb E^Y[Z]=0\).

title: Mean–variance & information
text:
Start with classical mean–variance
Let \(r\) be the vector of asset excess returns. With a reference asset available, risky weights \(w\) produce \(Z=w^\top r\); the remaining budget goes into the reference asset. Define
\[
\mu=\mathbb E^M[r],
\]
\[
\Sigma_M=\operatorname{Cov}^M(r).
\]
Classical mean–variance with risk penalty \(\lambda>0\) maximizes
\[
w^\top\mu-\frac\lambda2w^\top\Sigma_Mw.
\]
Both the mean and covariance are evaluated under the investor’s probability model. When \(\Sigma_M\) is positive definite and there are no constraints on risky positions,
\[
w^*=\frac1\lambda\Sigma_M^{-1}\mu.
\]
This formula does not check that terminal wealth stays nonnegative. Budget, leverage, short-sale and solvency constraints must be imposed separately. Under constraints, the solution is a quadratic program rather than this inverse-matrix formula.

title: Mean–variance & information
text:
The ordinary Taylor approximation
For \(Z\) near zero,
\[
\log(1+Z)=Z-\frac12Z^2+O(Z^3).
\]
Taking expectation under the investor’s belief gives
\[
T_M(Z)=\mathbb E^M[Z]-\frac12\mathbb E^M[Z^2].
\]
The penalty is a second moment, not just a variance:
\[
\mathbb E^M[Z^2]
=\operatorname{Var}^M(Z)+(\mathbb E^M[Z])^2.
\]
Thus the literal second-order approximation to expected log growth differs from classical mean–variance with \(\lambda=1\). It becomes unreliable near \(Z=-1\), where log utility diverges but the quadratic remains finite.

title: Mean–variance & information
text:
The book’s mixed-measure quadratic
The likelihood construction leads to another objective,
\[
J(Z)=\mathbb E^M[Z]-\frac12\mathbb E^Y[Z^2].
\]
Beliefs determine the expected reward; prices determine the quadratic geometry. Because \(\mathbb E^Y[Z]=0\), the penalty here also equals \(\tfrac12\operatorname{Var}^Y(Z)\).
This objective has an exact information interpretation. Set
\[
R=\frac{\mathbb P^M}{\mathbb P^Y},
\qquad
\chi^2=\mathbb E^Y[(R-1)^2].
\]
Completing the square gives
\[
J(Z)=\frac12\chi^2
-\frac12\mathbb E^Y[(G-R)^2].
\]
The first term is fixed. Maximizing \(J\) chooses the attainable payoff closest to the likelihood ratio \(R\) in squared error under the pricing measure. In a complete market, \(G=R\) is attainable and achieves the maximum \(\chi^2/2\) exactly.






NoteExact optimizer does not mean exact growth value



In a complete market, both log growth and this mixed quadratic select \(G=R\). Their objective values are different: the log optimum is \(D(\mathbb P^M\Vert\mathbb P^Y)\), whereas the quadratic optimum is \(\chi^2/2\). In a restricted asset menu, their best attainable portfolios can also differ.








NoteThe square-completion argument





Since \(\mathbb E^Y[Z]=0\),
\[
\mathbb E^M[Z]=\mathbb E^Y[(R-1)Z].
\]
For real numbers \(a,z\), the identity \(az-z^2/2=a^2/2-(z-a)^2/2\) applies state by state with \(a=R-1\). Taking \(\mathbb E^Y\) proves the formula. The continuous-state version requires \(R-1\) and \(Z\) to be square integrable.

title: Mean–variance & information
text:
Experiment with the approximation
The tool uses three scenarios and a portfolio of the reference asset and one risky asset. Its illustrative inputs are \(q=(0.30,0.40,0.30)\) and \(\mathbb P^X=(0.60,0.30,0.10)\). Belief strength moves the investor from \(q\) toward \((0.50,0.35,0.15)\). These are an asymmetric teaching example, chosen so the optimizers can differ.
Change belief strength, move the risky allocation \(w\) between zero and one, and compare exact growth with the ordinary Taylor and mixed quadratic objectives. Use each optimizer to see whether it chooses the same position.




Interactive comparison. It needs JavaScript.



Figure 1: The exact log criterion and two quadratic criteria share a zero value at the reference asset. Their differences grow as the payoff moves away from one. The tool uses the stated finite scenario model and the displayed allocation bounds.



The approximation depends on the size of statewise returns, not just on an apparently small average return. A small mean can coexist with a substantial probability of a nearly zero payoff.






NoteWhen do the two quadratic penalties agree locally?





Their difference is
\[
T_M(Z)-J(Z)
=-\frac12\mathbb E^Y[(R-1)Z^2].
\]
If both \(R-1\) and \(Z\) are uniformly of order \(\varepsilon\), this difference is of order \(\varepsilon^3\). In the same regime, both approximate expected log growth to second order. Small returns alone justify the ordinary Taylor expansion; using the pricing measure in the quadratic penalty also needs control of the difference between beliefs and prices, or the separate Pearson projection interpretation.

title: Mean–variance & information
section: From payoffs to a portfolio calculation
text:
From payoffs to a portfolio calculation
For excess-return vector \(r\) with \(\mathbb E^Y[r]=0\), define
\[
\Sigma_Y=\mathbb E^Y[rr^\top].
\]
The mixed objective becomes
\[
J(w)=w^\top\mu-\frac12w^\top\Sigma_Yw.
\]
With invertible \(\Sigma_Y\) and unconstrained risky weights, its solution is
\[
w^*=\Sigma_Y^{-1}\mu.
\]
The matrix resembles the classical covariance formula, but its entries come from \(\mathbb P^Y\). A singular matrix can reflect redundant assets; removing redundancy or solving the constrained program avoids treating its inverse as defined. Even when the matrix is invertible, an unrestricted projection can produce negative wealth. The portfolio laboratory keeps long-only cost weights and nonnegative payoffs.

title: Mean–variance & information
section: Two geometries for a restricted menu
text:
Two geometries for a restricted menu
In finite states, write \(p_i=\mathbb P^M(i)\), \(q_i=\mathbb P^Y(i)\) and \(v_i=\mathbb P^V(i)\). Then \(G(i)=v_i/q_i\), and the two projection problems are:



Objective
Mismatch minimized




Exact expected log growth
\(D(p\Vert v)\)


Mixed quadratic
\(\tfrac12\sum_i(v_i-p_i)^2/q_i\)



The second expression is a squared distance weighted by the fixed market distribution. It is generally not \(D_{\chi^2}(p\Vert v)\), whose denominator would be \(v_i\).
If the investor’s distribution is attainable, both mismatches can reach zero. Otherwise the geometry matters: the nearest feasible distribution in KL divergence need not be the nearest in market-weighted squared distance.
Continue: enter several asset densities and compare the resulting allocations in the portfolio laboratory.






NoteBook connection





Based on Chapter 3 of Jan Vecer’s Principles of Portfolio Choice: An Information-Theoretic, Likelihood-Based Perspective: “Mean-Variance Portfolio Optimization,” “Mean–variance as a quadratic approximation to log growth,” and the Pearson duality and projection results. The separate treatment of classical covariance, ordinary Taylor second moments and the mixed quadratic follows the distinctions made in that chapter.

title: Options as distributions
text:
A call pays in high-price states. A put pays in low-price states. Their densities show which observations the contracts emphasize, including how much weight each observation receives. Here we draw those densities continuously, using the normal model.
Throughout, prices are in units of the reference asset \(Y\), so \(Y(t)=1\). The underlying is \(X(t)\), and a strike \(K\) is fixed in those units. We return to currency prices below.

title: Options as distributions
text:
Three densities on one axis
Let \(z\) be the standardized normal observation at maturity \(T\), and set \(a=\sigma\sqrt T\). The market and asset assign it different normal laws:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f^Y(z)&=\varphi(z),\\
f^X(z)&=\varphi(z-a),
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(\varphi\) is the standard normal density. Thus \(z\) has mean zero under \(\mathbb P^Y\) and mean \(a\) under \(\mathbb P^X\), with variance one under both.
Dividing the densities determines the terminal price:
\[
\frac{X(T)}{X(0)}
=\frac{f^X(z)}{f^Y(z)}
=\exp\!\left(az-\frac{a^2}{2}\right).
\]
The observation is normal; the price is lognormal. This is the geometric Brownian motion model from the normal-model page, not a model in which the price itself is normally distributed.
Now choose an option payoff \(h(X(T))\). Its price and density are
\[
C(0)=\mathbb E^Y[h(X(T))],
\]
\[
f^C(z)=\frac{h(X(T))}{C(0)}\,f^Y(z).
\]
Multiply the market density by the payoff, then divide by its price. For a positive finite price, the result has area one. A call has no density below the exercise threshold; above it, larger payoffs receive more weight.

title: Options as distributions
text:
Draw the option’s view
Start with a call at strike 100. The blue and green curves are the two normal densities; the purple curve is the option’s induced density. Switch to a digital: its flat payoff above the strike conditions the market density on that region, without the call’s extra weighting toward larger gains.

The interactive density explorer requires JavaScript. With \(X(0)=K=100\), \(\sigma=0.25\) and \(T=1\), the call price is approximately \(9.948\). Its density is proportional to \(\bigl(100\varphi(z-0.25)-100\varphi(z)\bigr)^+\).

The density plot uses the normal observation \(z\) throughout. The separate payoff plot uses the terminal price \(X(T)\). Changing coordinates would change density heights; keeping a common observation axis makes the likelihood ratios directly visible.






NoteWhat this density means



\(\mathbb P^C\) describes the exposure built into one contract. It is not automatically the investor’s subjective forecast \(\mathbb P^M\). It also differs from recovering the underlying’s market distribution from a whole surface of option prices.

title: Options as distributions
section: A call price is a difference of two probabilities
text:
A call price is a difference of two probabilities
Let \(A=\{X(T)>K\}\). The call pays the underlying on \(A\), less the strike payment on the same event. Since \(X(T)f^Y=X(0)f^X\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
C(0)
&=X(0)\mathbb P^X(A)\\
&\quad-K\mathbb P^Y(A).
\end{aligned}
\]
The underlying payment is valued using the asset measure; the strike payment is valued using the reference measure. This identity holds before choosing any particular distribution.
Its density has an equally direct expression:
\[
f^C(z)
=\frac{\bigl(X(0)f^X(z)-Kf^Y(z)\bigr)^+}{C(0)}.
\]
The numerator is the positive part of the difference between two scaled densities. Its integral is the call price.

title: Options as distributions
text:
Black–Scholes from the normal tails
In the normal model, exercise means
\[
z>\frac{\log(K/X(0))}{a}+\frac a2.
\]
Write \(\Phi\) for the standard normal cumulative distribution function, and define
\[
\begin{aligned}
d(2)&=\frac{\log(X(0)/K)}{a}-\frac a2,\\
d(1)&=d(2)+a.
\end{aligned}
\]
Under \(\mathbb P^Y\), the observation has mean zero; under \(\mathbb P^X\), its mean is shifted by \(a\). The exercise probabilities are therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb P^Y(A)&=\Phi(d(2)),\\
\mathbb P^X(A)&=\Phi(d(1)).
\end{aligned}
\]
Substitute them into the two-measure price identity:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
C(0)&=X(0)\Phi(d(1))\\
&\quad-K\Phi(d(2)).
\end{aligned}}
\]
This is the Black–Scholes call formula in reference-asset units. The two normal probabilities have financial roles: one values delivery of the underlying, the other values payment of the strike. Neither probability is an investor’s personal forecast unless that investor chooses the corresponding measure.
For a put, use the complementary exercise region:
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(0)&=K\Phi(-d(2))\\
&\quad-X(0)\Phi(-d(1)).
\end{aligned}
\]
Subtracting yields put–call parity,
\[
C(0)-P(0)=X(0)-K.
\]






NoteThe familiar currency formula, with interest





Let the reference asset be a bank account \(B(t)=e^{rt}\) with constant rate \(r\) and \(B(0)=1\). For a non-dividend-paying stock with currency price \(S(t)\), we have \(X(t)=S(t)/B(t)\). A currency strike \(K^{\mathrm{cash}}\) at maturity becomes \(K=K^{\mathrm{cash}}e^{-rT}\) in reference units.
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
C^{\mathrm{cash}}(0)
&=S(0)\Phi(d(1))\\
&\quad-K^{\mathrm{cash}}e^{-rT}\Phi(d(2)),
\end{aligned}
\]
where
\[
\begin{aligned}
d(1)&=\frac{\log(S(0)/K^{\mathrm{cash}})+rT}{\sigma\sqrt T}\\
&\quad+\frac{\sigma\sqrt T}{2},\\
d(2)&=d(1)-\sigma\sqrt T.
\end{aligned}
\]
The discount factor appears when converting the currency strike into reference units. It was already accounted for by the choice of units above.

title: Options as distributions
section: Other payoffs, and a reference-asset reserve
text:
Other payoffs, and a reference-asset reserve
A digital call pays one unit on \(A\). Its price is \(\mathbb P^Y(A)=\Phi(d(2))\), and its induced distribution is \(\mathbb P^Y\) conditioned on \(A\).
A straddle combines a call and a put. Its density is the mixture of their densities with weights \(C(0)/(C(0)+P(0))\) and \(P(0)/(C(0)+P(0))\). The weights are fractions of the initial cost, even though the position holds one unit of each contract.
Calls, puts and digitals pay zero on entire regions. If an investor assigns positive probability to a zero-payoff region, committing all wealth to that option gives expected log performance \(-\infty\). The option density is still perfectly valid.
To retain a positive payoff floor, keep a fraction \(b\) of the budget in \(Y\) and allocate \(1-b\) to the option. The portfolio density is
\[
f^V(z)=b\,f^Y(z)+(1-b)f^C(z),
\]
and its gross payoff is at least \(b\). The explorer’s reserve control draws this mixture in gold. It is the same cost-weighted construction used in portfolio mixtures.
How could trading the underlying reproduce one of these payoffs? The discrete-hedging page compares a target density with the density implemented by rebalancing at finitely many dates.
